passages.text: A compendium of next-generation patient-derived models for diverse cancers

The development of new therapeutics and the validation of pathogenetic cancer mechanisms require representative laboratory models<sup><citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature11003" pmid="22460905" pmcid="PMC3320027" count="1">1</citation>,<citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1186-3" pmid="31068700" pmcid="PMC6697103" count="1">2</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>However, existing collections represent only a fraction of the diversity observed in human cancer<sup><citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1186-3" pmid="31068700" pmcid="PMC6697103" count="1">2</citation>-<citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41587-019-0055-9" pmid="30877282" count="1">4</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Recent technologies have enabled efficient in vitro model derivation (for example, tumour organoids)<citation rid="CR5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41568-018-0007-6" pmid="29692415" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>However, whether these maintain essential properties of patient tumours during long-term expansion has not been systematically investigated. <sentence_start/>Here we present results of a large-scale international programme-the Human Cancer Models Initiative-which involved the generation of a resource of 665 next-generation models from 2,780 donors with 25 cancer types and integrated tumour-model whole genome, exome, methylome and transcriptome analyses. <sentence_start/>The resource provides 522 models with comprehensive clinical data, 153 models of rare cancers and 71 models from participants with non-European ancestry. <sentence_start/>Analyses of 421 matched tumour-model pairs reveal high genetic (97.8%) and epigenetic (95%) concordance and define correlates of model discordance. <sentence_start/>Single-nucleus RNA sequencing of tumour-model pairs reveals subsets of models in which culture conditions significantly influence cell states. <sentence_start/>Finally, we characterize model preservation of extrachromosomal DNA and post-treatment mutational signatures to provide opportunities to study therapeutic resistance. <sentence_start/>This model repository is being made available to the community-including multimodal molecular profiling, clinical information and integrative software tools-thus providing a valuable resource for preclinical investigation of cancer pathogenesis and treatment response.

The international collaboration of the Human Cancer Models Initiative presents a comprehensive resource of next-generation cancer models from 2,780 donors with 25 cancer types and integrated tumour-model genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses.
Main

Major international projects have generated cancer atlases<sup><citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.2764" pmid="24071849" pmcid="PMC3919969" count="1">3</citation>,<citation rid="CR6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature08987" pmid="20393554" pmcid="PMC2902243" count="1">6</citation></sup> that have revealed many molecular underpinnings of human malignancies<sup><citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-1969-6" pmid="32025007" pmcid="PMC7025898" count="1">7</citation>-<citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2017.06.010" pmid="28753430" pmcid="PMC5667678" count="1">9</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Provocative hypotheses about most types of cancer have emerged, with each requiring preclinical validation to support both basic science and drug discovery. <sentence_start/>Well-characterized cancer models that maintain the fidelity of diverse human tumour types and clinical states are required for such validation<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-13-2971" pmid="24717177" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation>.

Efforts to genomically characterize large cohorts of cancer models have produced comprehensively annotated compendia of over 1,000 cell lines<sup><citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature11003" pmid="22460905" pmcid="PMC3320027" count="1">1</citation>,<citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1186-3" pmid="31068700" pmcid="PMC6697103" count="1">2</citation>,<citation rid="CR11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature11005" pmid="22460902" pmcid="PMC3349233" count="1">11</citation>,<citation rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nbt.3080" pmid="25485619" count="1">12</citation></sup>, which have enabled large-scale mapping of cancer dependencies<sup><citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2017.06.010" pmid="28753430" pmcid="PMC5667678" count="1">9</citation>,<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2016.06.017" pmid="27397505" pmcid="PMC4967469" count="1">13</citation>-<citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nbt.3460" pmid="26928769" pmcid="PMC5508574" count="1">16</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>However, existing cell lines typically exhibit limited phenotypic complexity, uncertain fidelity to the originating tumour specimen and inadequate clinical information<citation rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-018-0409-3" pmid="30089904" pmcid="PMC6522222" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation>.

Advances in the technology of cell culture, including biologically informed selection of defined growth factors and new plating methods, have facilitated the development of new patient-derived models<sup><citation rid="CR5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41568-018-0007-6" pmid="29692415" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="CR18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-1154" pmid="28331002" pmcid="PMC5413423" count="1">18</citation>-<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-18-0474" pmid="30213835" pmcid="PMC6365285" count="1">25</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>However, reports suggest that only a minority of such models could be indefinitely propagated and distributed.

Here we present the generation and comprehensive genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic characterization of 665 fully accessible patient-derived organoid, neurosphere and cell line models, which were created as part of the international Human Cancer Models Initiative (HCMI). <sentence_start/>Companion papers<sup><citation rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-026-10830-y" pmcid="PMC13581617" pmid="42557320" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-026-10843-7" pmcid="PMC13581591" pmid="42557315" count="1">27</citation></sup> demonstrate the utility of HCMI models for the systematic evaluation of gene essentiality and drug sensitivity.
Generation of 665 cancer models

Between 2016 and 2021, 2,780 patients from the United States, United Kingdom, Italy and the Netherlands consented to participate in the HCMI study (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). <sentence_start/>Active attempts were made to include diverse tumour types and patients from under-represented populations (Supplementary Methods, ‘Human subjects protocol’). <sentence_start/>Tissue samples were transferred to Cancer Model Development Centers at the Broad Institute, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Weill Cornell Medicine, Stanford University, the Hubrecht Institute and the University of Verona ARC-Net Research Centre (Supplementary Table 1) for model generation, with additional models derived and contributed by the Wellcome Sanger Institute.<sentence_start/>Fig. 1

Model derivation techniques varied by tumour type, sample type and model-derivation centre (Supplementary Methods, ‘CMDC model development’, and Supplementary Table 1). <sentence_start/>After several sequential passages, cultures were subjected to genomic-based quality control, authentication and subsequently banked for distribution (Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. <sentence_start/>1 and 2).

This process generated 665 models from 637 patients representing 25 distinct human malignancies (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Tables 1 and 2 and Supplementary Note 2). <sentence_start/>Success rates varied by tumour type, clinical stage and tissue type, and were affected by sample quality. <sentence_start/>Among the successful models, most were derived from adult donors (<italic>n</italic> = 622; 93.5%), but paediatric and adolescent donors were also represented (<italic>n</italic> = 43; 6.5%). <sentence_start/>Moreover, 23% of the successful models (<italic>n</italic> = 153) were of rare cancer types ( ). <sentence_start/>Models were established from primary tumours (<italic>n</italic> = 394; 59.2%) and metastatic lesions (<italic>n</italic> = 250; 37.6%) (Fig. 1b). <sentence_start/>Overall, 78% of models (<italic>n</italic> = 519) are three-dimensional (3D) organoid cultures, 6% are 3D spheroid cultures (<italic>n</italic> = 37) and 16% are two-dimensional (2D) adherent patient-derived cell lines (<italic>n</italic> = 109) (Fig. 1d, Supplementary Table 1). <sentence_start/>Patient-matched peripheral blood or normal tissue samples and parental tumour tissue samples were obtained for 95% and 62% of models, respectively (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>A total of 399 models had complete data trios (tumour, mode, and blood or normal samples) (Supplementary Table 1). <sentence_start/>Validated models were banked and made available for distribution through the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC).

We also analysed tumours from 168 failed derivation attempts (Extended Data Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>Specifically, we compared molecular features of successful and failed derivations across the three largest tumour cohorts (colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), oesophageal adenocarcinoma (ESCA) and pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD)). <sentence_start/>Although tumour purity did not emerge as a significant covariate (Supplementary Fig. 3ab), failed tumour samples presented increased representation of states associated with DNA repair and the cell cycle, whereas successful tumour samples displayed greater representation of differentiation, stemness and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related programs (Supplementary Fig. 3c-f).

To improve the representation of under-represented populations, HCMI enabled enrolment through the network of Tissue Source Sites from the National Cancer Institute (Supplementary Methods, ‘Establishment of CMDCs’) and a direct-to-patient consent platform ( ). <sentence_start/>We estimated genetic ancestry across five continental groups (Fig. 1c) (Methods, ‘Genetic ancestry estimation’). <sentence_start/>Across the cohort, the predominant ancestry groups were European (85%), African (6.5%), East Asian (3.7%), admixed American (2.5%) and South Asian (2.3%). <sentence_start/>Overall, 71 models are from primarily non-European ancestry donors. <sentence_start/>Some participants showed complex ancestry admixtures (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Previous modelling efforts lack systematic clinical annotations for each model. <sentence_start/>Here extensive clinical data, including treatment histories, were collected for 78% (<italic>n</italic> = 522) of the models (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>Data included patient overall survival (74% of models, with overall survival range of 0-34 years), treatments received before and after tissue procurement and post-therapy surival (median follow-up of 1.5 years) (Fig. 1e). <sentence_start/>A total of 318 models were generated from treatment-naive tissue samples, and 168 were generated from patients who had received previous therapy (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 1).
Evaluation of genomic fidelity

For the 421 models with matched parental tumours, we first evaluated DNA-level concordance. <sentence_start/>We compared ploidy and consensus copy number calls from tumour-model pairs using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) (Methods, ‘Genome sequencing: copy number’). <sentence_start/>For the 420 models for which purity values could be ascertained, 406 models had an estimated tumour purity of >80%, and very few (<italic>n</italic> = 9) models showed patterns of aneuploidy distinct from parental tumours. <sentence_start/>This result suggests that subclonal outgrowth is uncommon (Extended Data Fig. 2a-c). <sentence_start/>Moreover, 361 among 388 of the models with paired tumours exhibited a DNA loss of heterozygosity (LOH) concordance that exceeded 80% (average of 94%) (Fig. 2a).Fig. 2

Next, we evaluated concordance of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and insertions and deletions (indels). <sentence_start/>A median of 82.4% of SNVs and indels were shared between tumour and normal pairs (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 2d). <sentence_start/>Several low-concordance cases were associated with low tumour purity or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedding (FFPE) of tumours producing sequencing artefacts (Fig. 2a and Methods (‘Biospecimen processing and quality control’)). <sentence_start/>Five tumour-model pairs stood out as markedly discordant (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f). <sentence_start/>These included two unique PAAD tumour-model pairs in which distinct <italic>KRAS</italic><italic><sup>G12</sup></italic> mutations were observed between the tumour and the model. <sentence_start/>This result probably reflects the multifocal and polyclonal nature of PAAD (Supplementary Note 3).

We next assessed SNV mutational signatures by computing trinucleotide signature scores and cosine similarity between each tumour-model pair (Methods, ‘Analysis methods: Mutation signature’). <sentence_start/>We observed well-known signatures for specific tumour types (Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 2), which indicated that models retained relevant exposure signatures. <sentence_start/>The consistency was significantly higher than expected by chance (Fig. 2b). <sentence_start/>In the few pairs (<italic>n</italic> = 35; 8% of the total) with discordant signature profiles (cosine similarity < 0.9), no mutational signatures were consistently enriched in the models, which suggests that discordance was unlikely to arise from ex vivo culture (Extended Data Fig. 3b). <sentence_start/>These observations suggest that HCMI models faithfully recapitulate mutational signatures.

We next assessed whole-genome doubling (WGD) between tumour and model pairs. <sentence_start/>Most models recapitulated tumour WGD status (88%) (Fig. 2c), and the tumour-model ploidy was significantly correlated (Pearson’s correlation <italic>r </italic>= 0.53, <italic>P</italic> = 1.84 × 10<sup>−29</sup>; Fig. 2d). <sentence_start/>In 10% of the pairs, WGD was detected in the model but not the matched tumour, whereas WGD was seldom detected in the tumour but not the model (2% of cases) (Fig. 2c). <sentence_start/>SNV-based analyses indicated that WGD events detected only in models occurred later in the mutational timeline (<italic>P</italic> = 0.047, one-sided Mann-Whitney <italic>U</italic>-test). <sentence_start/>This finding is consistent with culture-associated clonal selection or spatial sampling variation. <sentence_start/>(Extended Data Fig. 3c), and provides support that tumour genomic structure is preserved.

Finally, we sought to confirm that well-known driver events were conserved. <sentence_start/>Across all tumour-specific driver events analysed, 81% of tumour events were retained in the models (Fig. 2e). <sentence_start/>Concordance was highest for canonical alterations in <italic>BRAF</italic> (skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM)), <italic>KRAS</italic> (PAAD), <italic>APC</italic> (COAD and rectum adenocarcinoma (READ)) and <italic>TP53</italic> (ESCA). <sentence_start/>Consistent with the literature for glioblastoma (GBM)<sup><citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-11-3084" pmid="22316604" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="3258189" count="1">29</citation></sup>, 80% of cases with extrachromosomal <italic>EGFR</italic> amplification showed higher <italic>EGFR</italic> copy number in the tumour than in the matched models (Extended Data Fig. 3d). <sentence_start/>On average, we detected a relatively lower level of concordance in extrachromosomal DNAs (ecDNAs) between tumour and model pairs, with 93 out of 212 (43.9%) of ecDNAs being model-specific and 69 out of 212 (32.5%) being tumour-specific (Fig. 2f). <sentence_start/>We attribute most of this discordance to low sequencing coverage (Extended Data Fig. 3e). <sentence_start/>However, differences in in vivo and ex vivo growth conditions may select for or against ecDNA amplification, as previously observed<citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-022-01177-x" pmid="36123406" pmcid="PMC9534767" count="1"><sup>30</sup></citation>.

In aggregate, 22 (5%) models were deprioritized for further interrogation owing to low purity. <sentence_start/>These models were excluded from subsequent analyses in this paper, which led to a collection of 643 prioritized HCMI models. <sentence_start/>In aggregate, our analyses confirmed that despite being passaged in culture for at least 1 year (Supplementary Methods, ‘Biospecimen collection and establishment of in vitro cultures’), most HCMI models (97.8%) retained at least two and often all four of the DNA-based features that we evaluated herein (driver mutations, mutational signatures, WGD and ploidy) (Fig. 2g).
Epigenetic and transcriptomic fidelity

We next evaluated epigenetic and transcriptional fidelity (Methods (‘Transcriptional relatedness measurements’) and Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>First, for the 201 tumour-model pairs for which DNA methylation profiles were available, we found that 190 paired distances (95%) were smaller than expected by random chance (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.1; Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>DNA methylation similarity was positively correlated with estimated tumour purity (Pearson’s correlation <italic>r</italic> = 0.33, <italic>P</italic> < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 4a). <sentence_start/>Overall, 9 out of 11 models with apparent epigenetic discordance were derived from tumours for which tissue purity estimates were below 60%, which suggests that this result is due to artefactual rather than biological discordance.<sentence_start/>Fig. 3

We next evaluated transcriptional concordance in 297 tumour-model pairs using Celligner<citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-20294-x" pmid="33397959" pmcid="PMC7782593" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation> (Methods, ‘Transcriptional relatedness measurements: Celligner’). <sentence_start/>Celligner identified 242 pairs (81%) as significantly concordant (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>Five additional computational methods further confirmed concordance (Fig. 3c, Methods, Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>Of the 286 models assessed by at least 4 of the 6 independent similarity metrics, only 1 model (HCM-CSHL-0255-C18) was considered non-concordant by 3 methods. <sentence_start/>Overall, 263 (92%) models were identified as discordant by no more than 1 method (Fig. 3c), a result that supports their ability to recapitulate key transcriptional states. <sentence_start/>Subsequent RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) profiling of 14 additional models, expanded independently at ATCC, did not reveal significant differences (paired <italic>t</italic>-test, <italic>P</italic> = 0.13; Extended Data Fig. 4c). <sentence_start/>These data show that most HCMI models preserve the transcriptional state of their parental tumours.

Several pan-cancer and cohort-specific molecular subtype stratifications of tumour samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)<citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.2764" pmid="24071849" pmcid="PMC3919969" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> have been proposed. <sentence_start/>These include a 106-subtype stratification based on subtypes defined in the original TCGA publications for each cohort (here, referred to as the tumour molecular pathology (TMP) subtypes<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2024.12.002" pmid="39753139" pmcid="PMC11949768" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation>) and a 112-subtype stratification by multi-omics master-regulator analysis (MOMA)<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2020.11.045" pmid="33434495" pmcid="PMC8103356" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation>, which is based on activities of master regulator proteins. <sentence_start/>Of all the tumour-model pairs in HCMI, a subset (<italic>n</italic> = 272 out of 297, 92%) could be classified on the basis of both TMP and MOMA subtypes (Supplementary Table 3).

Tumours and models from 160 (59%) and 177 (65%) of cases had identical TMP or MOMA classifications, respectively. <sentence_start/>In total, 228 tumour-model pairs (84%) were coherently classified by at least 1 of the 2 methods (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 4d). <sentence_start/>As expected, tumour-model pairs with high fidelity and identical TMP or MOMA subtypes generally displayed strong master regulator conservation (Fig. 3e). <sentence_start/>These results further confirm that most of the HCMI models are biologically relevant proxies.

Culture media have been shown to influence transcriptional states<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2021.11.017" pmid="34890551" pmcid="PMC8822455" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>We therefore investigated this aspect and observed that GBM models propagated in NeuroCult NS-A basal (NSA) medium were significantly more similar to their parental tumours than those cultured in Propagenix conditioned medium (Fisher’s exact test, <italic>P</italic> = 1.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup>; Fig. 3f). <sentence_start/>Expression differences were driven by the differential expression of established mesenchymal and proneural GBM lineage markers<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.18632/oncotarget.18363" pmid="29088733" pmcid="PMC5650288" count="1"><sup>35</sup></citation> (Fig. 3g, Extended Data Fig 4e and Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>Consistent with these findings, gene set enrichment analysis<citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.0506580102" pmid="16199517" pmcid="PMC1239896" count="1"><sup>36</sup></citation> identified EMT as differential, which suggests that the type of medium used for culture can influence the transition of GBM cells from proneural to mesenchymal<citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature08712" pmid="20032975" pmcid="PMC4011561" count="1"><sup>37</sup></citation> (Extended Data Fig. 4f and Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>We further evaluated these observed effects of medium conditions by single-nucleus transcriptional analysis (see below).

We performed medium-switching experiments (Supplementary Fig. 5a). <sentence_start/>When the GBM model HCM-BROD-0416-C71 was cultured in formulated-conditioned medium, it adopted new morphology (Fig. 3h), reduced nuclear SOX2 intensity (Supplementary Fig. 5b-d) and cell-state-related transcriptional changes (Fig. 3i and Supplementary Fig. 5e). <sentence_start/>Together, these findings indicate that serum-driven programs in GBM may exhibit plasticity. <sentence_start/>We did not observe major influences of media in other cancer model lineages beyond GBM (Supplementary Fig. 6a,b). <sentence_start/>As expected, we found that integrative master regulator and pathway analyses across seven core components of medium revealed modest transcriptional influences of serum, WNT and TGFβ inhibitor supplementation (Supplementary Fig. 6c,d).

Taken together, data from DNA-based and RNA-based analyses show that the majority of HCMI tumour-model pairs were concordant genetically (98%, 365 out of 373) and transcriptionally (92%, 263 out of 286). <sentence_start/>Consistent with previous reports<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2021.11.017" pmid="34890551" pmcid="PMC8822455" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation>, media emerged as a potential contributor to occasional transcriptional discordance.
HCMI expands model diversity

Recent studies have shown that the OncoMatch algorithm<sup><citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-22-0342" pmid="36374194" pmcid="PMC9905319" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-22-1020" pmid="37061969" pmcid="PMC10239356" count="1">39</citation></sup> can help identify translational-relevant models on the basis of conservation of master regulator activity<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2020.11.045" pmid="33434495" pmcid="PMC8103356" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Thus, for each TCGA sample, we tested whether HCMI, CCLE or the combined repositories (HCMI-CCLE) had at least one high-fidelity, histology-matched model (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 5f). <sentence_start/>HCMI outperformed CCLE in modelling 11 out of 19 cancer types (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted <italic>P</italic> < 0.05 by a two-sided Mann-Whitney <italic>U</italic>-test). <sentence_start/>By contrast, CCLE outperformed HCMI in six cancer types; however, four out of these six, were HCMI cohorts with a small number of models (<italic>n</italic> ≤ 10) (Extended Data Fig. 5f).

When HCMI and CCLE models were combined, the fraction of TCGA tumours for which a high-fidelity model was available increased, resulting in 77.3% (<italic>n</italic> = 6,902) of TCGA tumours having at least 1 high-fidelity model (normalized enrichment score (NES) ≥ 10). <sentence_start/>Thus, HCMI and CCLE are complementary resources for modelling human cancers.

Discussion

Here we presented the generation and comprehensive molecular characterization of 665 human cancer models and 581 tumours (413 that produced models and 168 from failed derivation attempts), together with detailed clinical characterization of the patients who donated tumour specimens. <sentence_start/>Notably, such models maintained high concordance with the primary tumour with respect to DNA alterations (97.8%) and RNA expression (92%), despite being cultured for a year or longer ex vivo. <sentence_start/>This fact and the scale of the resource provide new opportunities for the scientific community to investigate the therapeutic consequences of a wide range of genetic alterations and transcriptional states. <sentence_start/>For example, the two companion papers<sup><citation rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-026-10830-y" pmcid="PMC13581617" pmid="42557320" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-026-10843-7" pmcid="PMC13581591" pmid="42557315" count="1">27</citation></sup> demonstrate that the HCMI models are indeed suitable for high-throughput characterization of genetic dependencies using genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9-based screens and systematic assessments of drug sensitivity.

Cell lines and organoid cultures have important limitations, several of which are documented herein. <sentence_start/>Moreover, a growing body of literature<sup><citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2021.11.017" pmid="34890551" pmcid="PMC8822455" count="1">34</citation>,<citation rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-15548-7" pmid="32249764" pmcid="PMC7136203" count="1">53</citation>-<citation rid="CR55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fbioe.2020.00911" pmid="32850750" pmcid="PMC7417654" count="1">55</citation></sup> indicates that components of tissue culture media are key drivers of cell-state plasticity in cancer models. <sentence_start/>For example, our demonstration that NSA medium maintains the transcriptional states of GBM tumours, whereas other media do not, are reminiscent of recent reports that describe a similar influence of growth medium on cell states of pancreatic cancer models<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2021.11.017" pmid="34890551" pmcid="PMC8822455" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Such cell-state plasticity can be reversible, which suggests that models that have transcriptionally shifted can be converted into a state that is more faithful to the tumour by changing ex vivo growth conditions before experimentation.

The HCMI models are well suited to the systematic, scalable discovery of new targets and mechanisms of cancer. <sentence_start/>However, the absence of stromal and immune cells in the HCMI models limits their applicability in the study of immune responses; other model formats will be needed to fill this gap. <sentence_start/>Despite this limitation, in a subset of 25 models derived from patients previously treated with immunotherapy, we examined features previously associated with resistance phenotypes. <sentence_start/>Although these models lack an immune microenvironment, they may serve as a resource for studying tumour-intrinsic mechanisms of resistance and for identifying alternative therapeutic strategies.

Although most models were highly concordant with their parental tumours, approximately 4-8% of models seemed to be less concordant. <sentence_start/>For 16 tumour-model pairs, we performed snRNA-seq to clarify mechanisms of discordance at the single-cell level. <sentence_start/>These data supported the existence of three distinct mechanisms: (1) purification, in which loss of stromal and immune infiltrates present in the parent tumour are typically absent in cancer models; (2) selection, in which there is selective evolutionary outgrowth of a minor cancer subclone from the primary tumour; and (3) epigenomic plasticity, in which a transcriptional shift alters the relative representation of malignant cell states in models compared with the tumour of origin (in some cases, this was due to the culture medium). <sentence_start/>Despite the epigenomic plasticity of the cell state of some models, most models retained some representation of each of the cell states found in the parental tumour. <sentence_start/>This result suggests that single-cell analysis of HCMI models could gauge the influence of the most defined cellular states in response to drugs and to other perturbations.

Recent reports have highlighted the under-representation of publicly available cancer models of rare cancers, rare genotypes and cancers from ethnic and ancestry groups other than those of European origin<sup><citation rid="CR56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/cncr.32020" pmid="30865299" pmcid="PMC6541501" count="1">56</citation>,<citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2020.04.012" pmid="32396860" pmcid="PMC7328015" count="1">57</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>We took specific steps to address those challenges. <sentence_start/>These efforts were partially successful; the HCMI includes 153 rare cancer models and 38 models from patients of recent African descent.

However, we acknowledge that this diversity is insufficient and that further efforts are needed internationally to develop cancer models that avoid historical biases to ensure that research benefits all patients with cancer.

With the inclusion of the CCLE cell-line resource, over 2,000 publicly available cancer models now exist in the public domain ( ). <sentence_start/>However, in a post-TCGA and International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC)<citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41587-019-0055-9" pmid="30877282" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation> era, we recognize the scale of diversity of tumour subtypes, genetic alterations and phenotypic states that dictate the prognosis and treatment response of patients with cancer. <sentence_start/>Thus, we consider that the HCMI effort is only the beginning. <sentence_start/>That is, an order of magnitude expansion in publicly available cancer models may be needed to fully capture the heterogeneity of human cancers and to power the future of drug discovery for all patients.
Methods
Biospecimen processing and quality control

Before extracting nucleic acids, pathology quality control (QC) was performed on all frozen and FFPE tumours and normal specimens. <sentence_start/>From frozen tissue, a 30 mg or smaller piece was prepared, or an equivalent amount of scrolls were cut from a FFPE block, with sections stained with haematoxylin and eosin taken from the top and bottom of each specimen. <sentence_start/>The stained slides were scanned and their pathology reviewed to confirm that the tumour was consistent with the reported histology, and to assess the per cent tumour nuclei, per cent necrosis and other pathological features. <sentence_start/>The tumour nucleus and necrosis percentages from the top and bottom slides were averaged, and tumour specimens with an average of ≥50% tumour nuclei and ≤20% necrosis were submitted for nucleic acid extraction. <sentence_start/>Normal tissues were rejected if they had any detectable tumour cells.

DNA was extracted from normal blood and saliva specimens. <sentence_start/>DNA and RNA were co-extracted from tumours, solid normal tissues and cancer models. <sentence_start/>Before extraction, cancer models were first washed with ice-cold PBS to remove residual Matrigel. <sentence_start/>Frozen tissues and cancer models were homogenized using a Qiagen TissueLyser, and RNA and DNA were extracted using a modification of the DNA/RNA AllPrep kit (Qiagen). <sentence_start/>The homogenate was applied to a Qiagen DNA column, and the flow-through was processed using a mirVana miRNA Isolation kit (Ambion). <sentence_start/>FFPE specimens were deparaffinized and cells were lysed. <sentence_start/>The pellet underwent DNA extraction using an AllPrep FFPE kit (Qiagen), whereas the supernatant underwent RNA extraction using a Highpure miRNA kit (Roche). <sentence_start/>Blood specimens were extracted using a QiaAmp DNA Blood Midi kit (Qiagen), and saliva was extracted using a Gentra Puregene Buccal Cell kit (Qiagen).

DNA was quantified by PicoGreen assay and RNA was quantified by measuring the absorbance at 260 nm with a UV spectrophotometer. <sentence_start/>DNA quality was assessed by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis to confirm high-molecular-weight fragments. <sentence_start/>RNA was analysed using a RNA6000 Nano assay (Agilent) on an Agilent Bioanalyzer, which returns an RNA integrity number (RIN) for RNA from frozen tissues, or a DV200 for RNA extracted from FFPE specimens. <sentence_start/>All extracted DNA was subjected to a custom Sequenom single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) panel or an AmpFISTR Identifiler (Applied Biosystems) to verify that all specimens representing a case were derived from the same patient.
Genome sequencing
Data processing

The Genomics Data Commons (GDC) DNA-seq alignment pipeline<citation rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-021-21254-9" pmid="33619257" pmcid="PMC7900240" count="1"><sup>59</sup></citation>, was used to map WGS reads to a customized version of GRCh38. <sentence_start/>In brief, reads were aligned using BWA-MEM (v.0.7.15)<citation rid="CR60" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.6084/m9.figshare.963153.v1" count="1"><sup>60</sup></citation>, followed by sorting, merging and duplicate-marking using Picard Tools (v2.26.10). <sentence_start/>Base quality scores were recalibrated using GATK (v.3.7.0)<citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.107524.110" pmid="20644199" pmcid="PMC2928508" count="1"><sup>58</sup></citation> and BQSR. <sentence_start/>Sample contamination levels were estimated using GATK ContEst, and samples with contamination levels exceeding 4% were excluded from further analyses.
SNV and indel calling

<italic>The New York Genome Center pipeline.</italic> <sentence_start/>The New York Genome Center (NYGC; v.6) somatic SNV-indel-calling pipeline<citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-019-55636-3" pmid="31836783" pmcid="PMC6911065" count="1"><sup>61</sup></citation> was run for each tumour-normal and model-normal pair, starting from the GDC-aligned BAM files. <sentence_start/>In brief, SNVs, multi-nucleotide variants (MNVs) and indels were called using MuTect2 (GATK v.4.0.5.1)<citation rid="CR62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/861054" count="1"><sup>62</sup></citation>, Strelka2 (v.2.9.3)<citation rid="CR63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41592-018-0051-x" pmid="30013048" count="1"><sup>63</sup></citation> and Lancet (v.1.0.7)<citation rid="CR64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s42003-018-0023-9" pmid="30271907" pmcid="PMC6123722" count="1"><sup>64</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Indels were also called using SvABA (v.0.2.12)<citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.221028.117" pmid="29535149" pmcid="PMC5880247" count="1"><sup>65</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Candidate indels predicted by Manta (v.1.4.0)<citation rid="CR66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btv710" pmid="26647377" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> were used as input to Strelka2, as per developer recommendations. <sentence_start/>Variants were merged across callers and annotated using Ensembl (v.93)<citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/30.1.38" pmid="11752248" pmcid="PMC99161" count="1"><sup>67</sup></citation>, COSMIC (v.86)<citation rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gky1015" pmid="30371878" pmcid="PMC6323903" count="1"><sup>47</sup></citation>, 1000Genomes (Phase3)<citation rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature15393" pmid="26432245" pmcid="PMC4750478" count="1"><sup>68</sup></citation>, ClinVar (201706)<citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkt1113" pmid="24234437" pmcid="PMC3965032" count="1"><sup>69</sup></citation>, PolyPhen (v.2.2.2)<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nmeth0410-248" pmid="20354512" pmcid="PMC2855889" count="1"><sup>70</sup></citation>, SIFT (v.5.2.2)<citation rid="CR71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nprot.2015.123" pmid="26633127" count="1"><sup>71</sup></citation>, FATHMM (v.2.1)<citation rid="CR72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.22225" pmid="23033316" pmcid="PMC3558800" count="1"><sup>72</sup></citation>, gnomAD (r.2.0.1)<citation rid="CR73" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>75</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>From the final callset of SNVs and indels, we filtered those that met the following criteria: occurred in two or more individuals in a panel of normal samples<citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-019-55636-3" pmid="31836783" pmcid="PMC6911065" count="1"><sup>61</sup></citation>; those that had a minor allele frequency (MAF) of at least 1% in 1000Genomes or in gnomAD; had a tumour VAF less than 0.0001; had a normal VAF greater than 0.2; had depth less than 2 in either the tumour or the normal sample; or a VAF in the normal sample greater than in the tumour sample. <sentence_start/>The aforementioned panel of normal samples was constructed from 242 unrelated individuals, of which 148 were sequenced using HiSeqX in the Illumina Polaris project<citation rid="CR76" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.225672.117" pmid="28887402" pmcid="PMC5668946" count="1"><sup>76</sup></citation>, 73 were sequenced using HiSeqX at the NYGC, 11 were sequenced using NovaSeq at the NYGC, and 10 were sequenced on both HiSeqX and NovaSeq platforms at NYGC.

<italic>Broad pipeline (whole-exome sequencing)</italic>.Whole-exome sequencing (WES) BAM files were processed as described in the section ‘Data processing’. <sentence_start/>Variant calling was performed as previously described<citation rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s43018-023-00533-y" pmid="37081260" pmcid="PMC10132986" count="1"><sup>77</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>SNVs were called using MuTect and small indels were called using Strelka. <sentence_start/>Tumour-in-normal contamination estimation was performed using deTiN, and cross-participant contamination was estimated using ContEst. <sentence_start/>WES variant calling was performed as previously described<citation rid="CR77" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s43018-023-00533-y" pmid="37081260" pmcid="PMC10132986" count="1"><sup>77</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>A similar pipeline was used for processing variant calls from WGS.

<italic>WashU pipeline</italic>. <sentence_start/>The somatic variant pipeline TinDaisy2 (v.2.6.2; ) was built around the common workflow language and rooted in the methods of an earlier GenomeVIP pipeline architecture<citation rid="CR78" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.211656.116" pmid="28522612" pmcid="PMC5538560" count="1"><sup>78</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>For both WGS and WES data, we used TinDaisy2 for calling both SNV and indel variants. <sentence_start/>In brief, aligned BAMs for tumour and normal samples were processed using VarScan (v.2.3.8)<citation rid="CR79" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.129684.111" pmid="22300766" pmcid="PMC3290792" count="1"><sup>79</sup></citation>, Strelka2 (v.2.9.10)<citation rid="CR63" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41592-018-0051-x" pmid="30013048" count="1"><sup>63</sup></citation>, Pindel<citation rid="CR80" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btp394" pmid="19561018" pmcid="PMC2781750" count="1"><sup>80</sup></citation> and MuTect (v.mutect-1.1.7)<citation rid="CR81" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nbt.2514" pmid="23396013" pmcid="PMC3833702" count="1"><sup>81</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Filtering was performed to retain calls with length < 100, normal VAF ≤ 0.02, tumour VAF ≥ 0.05, tumour read depth > 14 and normal read depth > 8. <sentence_start/>Only variants identified by at least two or more callers were retained. <sentence_start/>Following annotation using VEP 99 (ref. <citation rid="CR82" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.24298" pmid="34816521" pmcid="PMC7613081" count="1"><sup>82</sup></citation>), calls with a population allele frequency of <0.005 were retained, and those that are in dbSnP but not in COSMIC<citation rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gky1015" pmid="30371878" pmcid="PMC6323903" count="1"><sup>47</sup></citation> or ClinVar<citation rid="CR83" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkx1153" pmid="29165669" pmcid="PMC5753237" count="1"><sup>83</sup></citation> were excluded. <sentence_start/>Adjacent SNP variants were merged into double nucleotide polymorphisms and higher-order variants, and the resulting VCF output was normalized with bcftools (v.1.10.2)<citation rid="CR84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/gigascience/giab008" pmid="33590861" pmcid="PMC7931819" count="1"><sup>84</sup></citation>.

<italic>Consensus method</italic>. <sentence_start/>The workflow MergeParticipantVcfs was run for all participants in the cohort. <sentence_start/>First, single-pair VCFs and MAFs from the NYGC (v.6) somatic pipeline, the Broad somatic pipeline and the WashU somatic pipeline were prepared for merging with the MergeVcf workflow. <sentence_start/>Multi-allelic calls were split, MNVs were labelled and then split into SNVs, centre names were prepended to all annotations and indels were left-aligned and normalized. <sentence_start/>Prepared VCFs were merged using BCFTools<citation rid="CR84" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/gigascience/giab008" pmid="33590861" pmcid="PMC7931819" count="1"><sup>84</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>During the merge-normalization of variants, the merging of SNPs into indels was not allowed. <sentence_start/>We calculated allele depth, read depth and allele frequency from BAM pileups using a custom method as described previously desribed<citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-019-55636-3" pmid="31836783" pmcid="PMC6911065" count="1"><sup>61</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>MNVs were re-established. <sentence_start/>If a pipeline reported only a subset of the SNVs that constitute an MNV, then the SNVs were also reported as a possible variant.

The merged, pair-level VCFs were merged again in the same fashion as described above using the MergeParticipantVcfs workflow. <sentence_start/>Next, we ran the MergeParticipantVcfs workflow, MuTect2 (GATK v.4.0.5.1)<citation rid="CR62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/861054" count="1"><sup>62</sup></citation> on the multisample VCF, in forcecalling mode. <sentence_start/>A MuTect2 filter with read orientation metrics was run on the force-called results. <sentence_start/>The filtered MuTect2 calls were used to annotate the merged centre VCF. <sentence_start/>The final genotype was taken from the MuTect2 forcecalls and all other MuTect2 annotations were included with the prefix “Mutect2Multi_.”

The non-normal aliquots that the variant was called in, and the list of callers supporting the variant, were annotated in the VCF. <sentence_start/>Variants were also annotated using Ensembl variant effect predictor (v.97)<citation rid="CR67" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/30.1.38" pmid="11752248" pmcid="PMC99161" count="1"><sup>67</sup></citation> as well as the databases COSMIC (v.98)<citation rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gky1015" pmid="30371878" pmcid="PMC6323903" count="1"><sup>47</sup></citation>, 1000Genomes (Phase3)<citation rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature15393" pmid="26432245" pmcid="PMC4750478" count="1"><sup>68</sup></citation>, ClinVar (09012020)<citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkt1113" pmid="24234437" pmcid="PMC3965032" count="1"><sup>69</sup></citation>, Polyphen2 (v.2.2.2)<citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nmeth0410-248" pmid="20354512" pmcid="PMC2855889" count="1"><sup>70</sup></citation>, SIFT (v.5.2.2)<citation rid="CR71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nprot.2015.123" pmid="26633127" count="1"><sup>71</sup></citation>, FATHMM (v.2.1)<citation rid="CR72" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.22225" pmid="23033316" pmcid="PMC3558800" count="1"><sup>72</sup></citation>, gnomAD (Genomes (v.3.1.2) and Exomes (v.2.1.1))<citation rid="CR73" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7" pmid="32461654" pmcid="PMC7334197" count="1"><sup>73</sup></citation> and dbSNP (v.150)<citation rid="CR74" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/29.1.308" pmid="11125122" pmcid="PMC29783" count="1"><sup>74</sup></citation>.

The annotated calls were used as input for the MakePairHighConfidenceVcfs workflow and filtered into final HighConfidence VCFs. <sentence_start/>Calls were removed if MuTect2 failed the call. <sentence_start/>Calls were added for a pair if they had read support in all non-normal WGS BAMs for that participant (even if the variant was not formally called for this pair).
Copy number calling

<italic>Ascat method</italic>. <sentence_start/>Purity and ploidy estimates were generated for each tumour-normal and model-normal pair using AscatNGS (v.4.2.1)<citation rid="CR85" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/cpbi.17" pmid="27930809" pmcid="PMC6097604" count="1"><sup>85</sup></citation> using default parameters.

<italic>ABSOLUTE method</italic>. <sentence_start/>Copy number segmentation was performed using fragcounter and ReCapSeg, and subsequently with AllelicCapSeg. <sentence_start/>AllelicCapSeg output files were used as inputs for ABSOLUTE, with WES (when available) or WGS mutation calls used to infer allelic integer copy number profiles. <sentence_start/>All ABSOLUTE calls were manually curated to identify the ABSOLUTE with integer copy number states best aligning with the observed copy number values. <sentence_start/>In samples with no CNAs, the optimal ABSOLUTE solution was inferred from SNV multiplicity.

<italic>ReMixT method</italic>. <sentence_start/>We applied ReMixT<citation rid="CR86" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13059-017-1267-2" pmid="28750660" pmcid="PMC5530528" count="1"><sup>86</sup></citation> to predict allele-specific and clone-specific copy numbers from WGS samples according to previously described methods<citation rid="CR87" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.073" pmid="29754820" count="1"><sup>87</sup></citation>.

<italic>PURPLE method</italic>. <sentence_start/>For each tumour-normal or model-normal sample pair, we generated a B-allele frequency of heterozygous SNP sites using AMBER (v.3.5)<citation rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1689-y" pmid="31645765" pmcid="PMC6872491" count="1"><sup>88</sup></citation>, and we determined read depth ratios using COBALT (v.1.11)<citation rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1689-y" pmid="31645765" pmcid="PMC6872491" count="1"><sup>88</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>We integrated this information, together with somatic SNVs and structural variants (SVs) to estimate the purity, ploidy and copy number profile of the tumour using PURPLE (v.2.54)<citation rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1689-y" pmid="31645765" pmcid="PMC6872491" count="1"><sup>88</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Tumour and model samples that did not have a matched normal sample were processed in a similar manner, but with several version changes: AMBER (v.3.9), COBALT (v.1.13) and PURPLE (v.3.4). <sentence_start/>AMBER, COBALT and PURPLE were developed by the Hartwig Medical Foundation and are freely available on GitHub ( ).

<italic>HATCHet method</italic>. <sentence_start/>For each tumour-normal or model-normal sample pair, we ran HATCHet-2 (ref. <citation rid="CR89" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13059-024-03267-x" pmid="38773520" pmcid="PMC11110434" count="1"><sup>89</sup></citation>) and estimated purity and ploidy. <sentence_start/>We used default parameters, but with the following exceptions. <sentence_start/>The minimum and maximum number of states and state transition probability in the hidden Markov model were set to 20, 40 and 10<sup>−12</sup>, respectively, whereas ‘diploidbaf’ and ‘maxneutralshift’ parameters were both set to 0.06. <sentence_start/>The search space for the number of clones was between two and four. <sentence_start/>A Gurobi commercial optimizer was used as the preferred engine for solving integer linear programming.

<italic>Consensus method</italic>. <sentence_start/>For each sample, the ABSOLUTE solution for which values were nearest to the consensus purity and ploidy values was selected as the consensus copy number solution. <sentence_start/>In cases when the optimal ABSOLUTE purity and ploidy solution and the consensus purity and ploidy solutions were divergent, the consensus solution was still selected. <sentence_start/>ABSOLUTE forcecalling was performed using each selected purity and ploidy solution with the output being the segmented allelic copy number state at each genomic locus.
SV calling

<italic>NYGC pipeline</italic>. <sentence_start/>The NYGC (v.6) somatic SV-calling pipeline<citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-019-55636-3" pmid="31836783" pmcid="PMC6911065" count="1"><sup>61</sup></citation> was run for each tumour-normal and model-normal pair, starting from the GDC-aligned BAM files. <sentence_start/>In brief, SV breakpoints were called using SvABA (v.0.2.12)<citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.221028.117" pmid="29535149" pmcid="PMC5880247" count="1"><sup>65</sup></citation>, Manta (v.1.4.0)<citation rid="CR66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btv710" pmid="26647377" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> and Lumpy (v.0.2.13)<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/gb-2014-15-6-r84" pmid="24970577" pmcid="PMC4197822" count="1"><sup>90</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>We excluded SVs below 500 bp, merged the rest across callers using bedtools (v.2.26.0)<citation rid="CR91" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btq033" pmid="20110278" pmcid="PMC2832824" count="1"><sup>91</sup></citation>, pair-to-pair with the slop parameter set to 300 bp, and requiring the same strand orientation and at least 50% reciprocal overlap. <sentence_start/>SVs were annotated using 1000Genomes (Phase3)<citation rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature15393" pmid="26432245" pmcid="PMC4750478" count="1"><sup>68</sup></citation>, DGV<citation rid="CR92" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkt958" pmid="24174537" pmcid="PMC3965079" count="1"><sup>92</sup></citation>, gnomAD-SV<citation rid="CR93" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-2287-8" pmid="32461652" pmcid="PMC7334194" count="1"><sup>93</sup></citation> and the SV panel of normals (built from the same individuals as the NYGC SNV-indel pipeline) with bedtools pair-to-pair, using the same parameters as for the merge across callers. <sentence_start/>We removed from the final callset any SVs that overlapped variants in 1000Genomes, DGV, gnomAD-SV or the panel of normals.

<italic>Broad pipeline</italic>. <sentence_start/>SVs were called using Manta<citation rid="CR66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btv710" pmid="26647377" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation>, SvABA<citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.221028.117" pmid="29535149" pmcid="PMC5880247" count="1"><sup>65</sup></citation> and dRanger<citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.141382.112" pmid="23124520" pmcid="PMC3561864" count="1"><sup>94</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Breakpointer<citation rid="CR94" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.141382.112" pmid="23124520" pmcid="PMC3561864" count="1"><sup>94</sup></citation> was used to refine breakpoint locations of called variants. <sentence_start/>The same SV had to have been called across at least two of Manta, SvABA and dRanger (using a clustering window of 350 bp to match the SV to the same event) to show up in the final callset. <sentence_start/>Certain filters were applied across various steps of the pipeline based on span, mapping quality and reads of support for SV events.

<italic>WashU pipeline</italic>. <sentence_start/>We used Manta (v.1.6.0)<citation rid="CR66" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btv710" pmid="26647377" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> for calling SVs on matched tumour-normal WGS data. <sentence_start/>We then filtered results to retain variants that met the following criteria: (1) the sample site depth was less than 3× the median chromosome depth near one or both variant breakends; (2) the somatic score was greater than 30; and (3) for a small variant (<1,000 bases) in the normal sample, the fraction of reads with MAPQ0 around the breakend did not exceed 0.4. <sentence_start/>We then converted VCF files to BEDPE format with svtools (v.0.5.1)<citation rid="CR95" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btz492" pmid="31218349" pmcid="PMC6853660" count="1"><sup>95</sup></citation> ( ).

<italic>MSKCC pipeline</italic>. <sentence_start/>We identified SVs using deStruct (v.0.4.18)<citation rid="CR96" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/117523" count="1"><sup>96</sup></citation> and LUMPY (v.0.2.12)<citation rid="CR90" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/gb-2014-15-6-r84" pmid="24970577" pmcid="PMC4197822" count="1"><sup>90</sup></citation>, retaining only the breakpoints called by both methods. <sentence_start/>We applied filtering based on the following criteria: inter-breakpoint distances of ≤30 bp; deletions smaller than 1,000 bp; breakpoints with fewer than 5 supporting reads in the tumour sample; or any read support in the matched normal sample.

<italic>EMBL-EBI pipeline</italic>. <sentence_start/>For tumour-normal and model-normal sample pairs, somatic SVs were called using GRIDSS2 (v.2.12.0)<citation rid="CR97" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13059-021-02423-x" pmid="34253237" pmcid="PMC8274009" count="1"><sup>97</sup></citation>, annotated with RepeatMasker (v.4.1.2)<citation rid="CR98" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19274634" doi="10.1002/0471250953.bi0410s25" count="1"><sup>98</sup></citation>, and kraken2 (v.2.1.2)<citation rid="CR99" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41596-022-00738-y" pmid="36171387" pmcid="PMC9725748" count="1"><sup>99</sup></citation> and filtered with GRIPSS (v.1.9)<citation rid="CR100" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.xgen.2022.100112" pmid="36776527" pmcid="PMC9903802" count="1"><sup>100</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The final somatic SV set was further refined and annotated with the copy number profile estimated using PURPLE (v.2.54)<citation rid="CR88" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1689-y" pmid="31645765" pmcid="PMC6872491" count="1"><sup>88</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>SVs and copy number profiles were visualized using the ReConPlot R package (v.1.0)<citation rid="CR101" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btad719" pmid="38058190" pmcid="PMC10710371" count="1"><sup>101</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Tumour and model samples without a matched normal sample were processed in a similar manner but with several version changes: GRIPSS (v.2.0.1) and PURPLE (v.3.4).

<italic>Consensus method</italic>. <sentence_start/>Consensus SVs from the NYGC Broad, WashU, MSKCC and EMBL-EBI were identified as previously described<citation rid="CR102" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1913-9" pmid="32025012" pmcid="PMC7025897" count="1"><sup>102</sup></citation> using bedtools pair2pair with minor modifications. <sentence_start/>The original consensus algorithm used single-caller VCFs as inputs, whereas the modified pipeline uses multicaller consensus inputs from each centre. <sentence_start/>Moreover, the original pipeline used a slop value of 400, whereas the modified pipeline uses a slop value of 50. <sentence_start/>SVs called by pipelines from two or more analysis centres were accepted into the final SV consensus.
Purity and ploidy

<italic>ESTIMATE</italic>. <sentence_start/>Tumour purity was computed according to the ESTIMATE algorithm<citation rid="CR103" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms3612" pmid="24113773" pmcid="PMC3826632" count="1"><sup>103</sup></citation>, which generates a composite ESTIMATE score that represents the quantification of predefined gene signatures of non-tumour components (stromal and immune) in gene expression data. <sentence_start/>Tumour purity was then inferred using the following formula: tumour purity = cos (0.6049872018 + 0.0001467884 × ESTIMATE score).

<italic>Consensus purity and ploidy</italic>. <sentence_start/>We computed consensus tumour and model purity and ploidy from the purity and ploidy values from five DNA-based copy number callers (Ascat, ABSOLUTE, ReMixT, PURPLE and Hatchet) and purity values from a sixth RNA-based caller (ESTIMATE). <sentence_start/>Consensus purity was computed using an iterative process wherein the mean purity across all callers was first computed. <sentence_start/>If the individual purity values across all six purity callers fell within ±0.2 of the mean purity, then the mean purity was accepted as the consensus purity. <sentence_start/>If one or more callers fell outside the window, then the furthest caller from the mean was removed and the mean ploidy was recomputed. <sentence_start/>This process was repeated until all remaining callers converged on a consensus purity value or when fewer than three callers remained. <sentence_start/>In the latter case, the purity value was accepted as the value from ABSOLUTE or, in cases when there was no ABSOLUTE value, from PURPLE.

Ploidy values for each individual caller were first binned into ploidy classes: haploid (ploidy < 1.5), diploid (1.5 ≤ ploidy < 2.5), triploid (2.5 ≤ ploidy < 3.5) or tetraploid (≥3.5). <sentence_start/>If values from three or more callers fell in the same ploidy class, then the median ploidy from all callers in that ploidy class was taken as the consensus ploidy. <sentence_start/>If there was no agreement between three or more callers, then the ploidy value from ABSOLUTE was accepted as the consensus ploidy value or, in cases when there was no ABSOLUTE value, the value from PURPLE was accepted as the consensus ploidy value. <sentence_start/>All consensus purity and ploidy values went through subsequent manual curation and the ABSOLUTE solution was selected in cases when the consensus purity and ploidy values poorly reflected the underlying copy number states.
Analysis methods

<italic>Tumour-model SNV concordance</italic>. <sentence_start/>SNVs included in concordance analysis were filtered for variants with VAF > 0.15 or variants for which all non-normal aliquots contained read support.

<italic>Tumour-model LOH concordance</italic>. <sentence_start/>The LOH status for all tumour-model pairs was determined by examining whether the rounded minor copy number of each genomic bin was equal to zero. <sentence_start/>LOH status was then compared between the tumour and its corresponding model, assigning a value of 1 for concordance and 0 for discordance. <sentence_start/>The mean LOH concordance was subsequently calculated across all equal-sized bins, which provided a single LOH concordance value for each tumour-model pair.

<italic>WGD inference</italic>. <sentence_start/>We determined WGD status by assessing genome-wide CNAs. <sentence_start/>First, we calculated the fraction of the genome that was affected by copy number gains, weighting each segment by its genomic length. <sentence_start/>We evaluated the extent of duplication based on thresholds for copy number amplification across the genome. <sentence_start/>Samples in which a majority of the genome exhibited copy number gains beyond a defined threshold were classified as having undergone a single WGD event, whereas those surpassing a higher threshold were assigned multiple WGD events.

<italic>Mutation signature</italic>. <sentence_start/>SNV mutational signatures were computed using SignatureAnalyzer (GPU version)<sup><citation rid="CR104" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13059-019-1836-7" pmid="31675989" pmcid="PMC6823959" count="1">104</citation>,<citation rid="CR105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms9866" pmid="26638776" pmcid="PMC4686820" count="1">105</citation></sup> with the COSMIC single-base substitution signature reference comprising 96 mutational signatures. <sentence_start/>During mutational signature factorization, a set of 51 non-redundant mutational signatures were selected. <sentence_start/>For each tumour and matched model, we generated per-sample mutational signature profiles represented as exposure vectors across these 51 signatures. <sentence_start/>Concordance between tumours and their matched models (<italic>n</italic> = 440 pairs) was quantified in terms of the cosine similarity between their respective signature profiles. <sentence_start/>As a negative control, we generated random tumour-model pairings of equal number, both in the same tumour type and across different tumour types, and calculated cosine similarities for the randomized pairs.

<italic>Driver oncogene selection and classification</italic>. <sentence_start/>To assess the differences in the prevalence of driver mutations between tumour and model samples, we first curated a set of driver genes based on previous TCGA studies<citation rid="CR106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2018.02.060" pmid="29625053" pmcid="PMC6029450" count="1"><sup>106</sup></citation> (Supplementary Table 10). <sentence_start/>To determine the prevalence of SNVs, small indels and copy number variations (CNVs), we integrated the results from both SNV-indel and copy number analyses. <sentence_start/>Gene annotations for SNVs and indels were obtained through the discovery pipeline. <sentence_start/>Only mutations with a predicted impact of moderate or high, as defined in the Ensembl calculated gene consequences table, were included in downstream analyses. <sentence_start/>An additional mutation category included upstream promoter missense mutations in the <italic>TERT</italic> gene. <sentence_start/>Gene-level CNVs were annotated by calculating the mean copy number across the genomic span of each gene. <sentence_start/>Only genes with high-level amplifications or homozygous deletions were included in the downstream analysis. <sentence_start/>A gene was classified as highly amplified if it met the following criteria: (1) sample ploidy ≥ 1.5; (2) either the gene copy number was ≥3 and ≥2 times the ploidy (adjusted by -0.5 if the sample was a model); or (3) the gene copy number was ≥7. <sentence_start/>Conversely, a gene was classified as having a homozygous deletion if its copy number was below 0.3.

For the final visualization in Fig. 2, mutations were classified as either gain-of-function (GOF) or loss-of-function (LOF). <sentence_start/>For each gene, only mutations that were found in both tumour and matched model samples (that is, shared in a tumour-model pair) were considered. <sentence_start/>Only mutations shared between tumour and matched model samples (that is, present in both) were considered for classification. <sentence_start/>If no shared mutations were identified for a given gene, it was labelled as unclassified. <sentence_start/>Mutation types were grouped as follows: LOF included homozygous deletions, truncating variants (frameshift indels, nonsense and splice-site mutations); GOF included missense mutations, high-level amplifications, <italic>TERT</italic> promoter mutations and in-frame insertions or deletions. <sentence_start/>A gene was labelled LOF if more than 15% of its shared mutations were LOF events, otherwise, it was labelled as GOF.

<italic>Power calculation</italic>. <sentence_start/>We calculated a measure of the power to detect model SNVs in a given tumour by considering the probability that model SNVs would be detected in the tumour, assuming that there were clonal and at one allelic copy. <sentence_start/>The expected VAF for a single-allelic clonal tumour mutation at a genomic position with tumour copy number <italic>T</italic> is given by Here <italic>N</italic> is the copy number at the given position of the contaminating cells, which was assumed to be two for autosomes. <sentence_start/>Then, assuming a binomial distribution of read counts and one read necessary to detect, the average power to detect a clonal SNV was calculated by where Binomial<sub>CDF</sub> is the binomial cumulative density function. <sentence_start/>Here <italic>C</italic><italic><sub>i</sub></italic> is the read coverage in the tumour at the position of the <italic>i</italic>th model SNV. <sentence_start/>This value is calculated by summing over all <italic>N</italic> SNV positions identified as having at least one alternative read in the model and any number of reads in the tumour. <sentence_start/>Only autosomal SNVs were considered for the power calculation.

<italic>ecDNA</italic>. <sentence_start/>Raw coverage was calculated from the GDC-aligned BAM files using fragCounter (v.1.0; ). <sentence_start/>These values were corrected using dryClean (v.1.0), a robust PCA-based method that separates the foreground from the background signal, which reduces noise and artefacts. <sentence_start/>It was run using a panel of 390 normal samples, which we built by selecting random normal samples across different datasets: ICGC DCC ESAD-UK<citation rid="CR107" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-018-0331-5" pmid="30718927" pmcid="PMC6420087" count="1"><sup>107</sup></citation>, TCGA<citation rid="CR108" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3101" pmid="25261935" pmcid="PMC4217527" count="1"><sup>108</sup></citation>, the MSKCC-WCM-NYGC HRD project<citation rid="CR109" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-023-06461-2" pmid="37587346" pmcid="PMC10482687" count="1"><sup>109</sup></citation>, The Cancer Alliance at NYGC<citation rid="CR110" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-023-01540-6" pmid="37945902" pmcid="PMC10703688" count="1"><sup>110</sup></citation>, the Hartwig Medical Foundation ( ), ICGC PanCancer Analysis of Whole Genomes<citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-1969-6" pmid="32025007" pmcid="PMC7025898" count="1"><sup>7</sup></citation>, CCLE<citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-019-1186-3" pmid="31068700" pmcid="PMC6697103" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation> and other publications<sup><citation rid="CR111" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2019.05.013" pmid="31155235" count="1">111</citation>-<citation rid="CR116" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pgen.1002772" pmid="22829774" pmcid="PMC3400581" count="1">116</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>These corrected values were used as inputs for CBS<citation rid="CR117" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/biostatistics/kxh008" pmid="15475419" count="1"><sup>117</sup></citation> to calculate the tumour-normal coverage ratio and to segment the genome into regions of similar copy number, thereby identifying potential amplifications and deletions. <sentence_start/>This information, together with the consensus purity and ploidy values and the consensus SVs, were used to construct junction-balanced genome graphs that had high-fidelity copy number profiles using JaBbA (v.1.1)<sup><citation rid="CR110" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-023-01540-6" pmid="37945902" pmcid="PMC10703688" count="1">110</citation>,<citation rid="CR118" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.006" pmid="33007263" pmcid="PMC7912537" count="1">118</citation></sup>.

GDC-aligned BAM files and JaBbA-derived copy number profiles were then used as input to the AmpliconSuite-pipeline (v.0.5.2)<citation rid="CR119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2024.05.06.592768" count="1"><sup>119</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>This pipeline is a wrapper for the AmpliconArchitect (v.1.3.r5)<citation rid="CR120" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-018-08200-y" pmid="30674876" pmcid="PMC6344493" count="1"><sup>120</sup></citation> and downstream AmpliconClassifier (v.0.5.3)<citation rid="CR119" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2024.05.06.592768" count="1"><sup>119</sup></citation> tools. <sentence_start/>As per developer recommendations, samples derived from the same patient (for example, paired tumour-models) were run as a group using GroupedAnalysisAmpSuite.py, using default parameters.

We then compared the resulting amplicon calls using the comparison tool feature_similarity.py, with default parameters. <sentence_start/>ecDNAs were considered concordant between tumour and model if the overlapping amplicons were classified the same way and had a Jaccard genomic interval similarity of ≧0.75. <sentence_start/>A Jaccard genomic interval similarity was calculated as the total length of the intersection of the amplicon footprints, divided by length of the union. <sentence_start/>We retained amplicon calls if the indicated filter was ‘none’. <sentence_start/>ecDNA calls, filtered by AmpliconArchitect, were ‘rescued’ back into the callset if they had a passing concordant ecDNA in the associated tumour or model.

Putative cyclic ecDNA reconstructions were generated using the AmpliconSuite-pipeline module Candidate AMplicon Path EnumeratoR. In brief, the tool searches each amplicon graph for the longest cyclic and non-cyclic paths, choosing paths that best explain the observed copy numbers, and filtering based on how well the best reconstruction fits the data. <sentence_start/>Reconstructions that passed were plotted using CycleViz ( ).

<italic>Clonal phylogenies</italic>. <sentence_start/>Force-called SNVs were input into pyclone and phyclone to generate clonal phylogenies. <sentence_start/>We excluded indels from the analysis. <sentence_start/>We annotated each SNV with the major and minor allele copy number of the encompassing segment from consensus copy number calling. <sentence_start/>SNV copy number and supporting read counts were input to pyclone-vi (v.0.1.6)<citation rid="CR121" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12859-020-03919-2" pmid="33302872" pmcid="PMC7730797" count="1"><sup>121</sup></citation>, which we ran with a beta-binomial observation model, 10 restarts and a maximum of 40 clusters. <sentence_start/>We removed clusters comprising less than 1% of all SNVs and clusters that were approximately 0.5 cancer cell fraction across all samples (cancer cell fraction range of 0.3-0.7). <sentence_start/>The resulting pyclone clusters were input to phyclone (v.0.5.1)<citation rid="CR122" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf344" pmcid="PMC12964358" pmid="40511985" count="1"><sup>122</sup></citation>, which we ran with a beta-binomial observation model, 16 chains, 100,000 iterations and outlier probability set to 0.1.

<italic>Genetic ancestry estimation</italic>. <sentence_start/>Ancestry proportion was determined using ADMIXTURE (v.1.3.0)<sup><citation rid="CR123" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.24072/pcjournal.503" count="1">123</citation>,<citation rid="CR124" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/gr.094052.109" pmid="19648217" pmcid="PMC2752134" count="1">124</citation></sup>, which used a maximum likelihood-based method to estimate the proportion of reference-population ancestries in a sample. <sentence_start/>To do this, we genotyped reference markers that we generated from 1,964 unrelated 1000Genomes project samples directly on the whole-genome samples using GATK pileup (v.3.4.0). <sentence_start/>We excluded individuals from the populations MXL (Mexican ancestry from Los Angeles, United States), ACB (African Caribbean in Barbados) and ASW (African ancestry in the Southwest United States) from the reference owing to their being putatively admixed. <sentence_start/>We further filtered the reference by using only SNP markers with a minimum MAF of 0.01 overall and 0.05 in at least one 1000Genomes continental population. <sentence_start/>Variants were also pruned on the basis of linkage disequilibrium using PLINK (v.1.9) with a window size of 500 kb, a step size of 250 kb and an r2 threshold of 0.2. <sentence_start/>The analysis resulted in a proportional breakdown of each sample into five continental populations (AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR and SAS) and 23 populations. <sentence_start/>We then categorized patients by the continental population of highest proportion.
DNA methylation and epigenetic fidelity
DNA methylation data

DNA methylation was evaluated using the Illumina HumanMethylationEPIC (EPICv1) array (Illumina). <sentence_start/>We downloaded raw IDAT files produced by the Illumina iScan system from the GDC data portal ( ). <sentence_start/>We calculated DNA methylation levels (<italic>β</italic> values) from the IDAT files using the openSesame pipeline with the default arguments implemented in the R package SeSAMe (v.1.18.4)<citation rid="CR125" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30085201" doi="10.1093/nar/gky691" pmcid="PMC6237738" count="1"><sup>125</sup></citation>.
Normal tissue methylation and probe selection

We used normal tissue DNA methylation data from external resources to investigate cancer-associated DNA methylation profiles. <sentence_start/>We had previously identified 146,385 CpGs that were unmethylated in eight normal tissue types (breast, adrenal gland, liver, lung, ovary, skin, blood and brain) on the EPICv1 array<citation rid="CR126" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s43018-022-00491-x" pmid="36585450" pmcid="PMC9886551" count="1"><sup>126</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>We processed additional ENCODE normal tissue DNA methylation data from 23 normal tissue samples from the gastrointestinal tract, including oesophagus (muscularis mucosa <italic>n</italic> = 4, squamous epithelium <italic>n</italic> = 4), stomach (<italic>n</italic> = 3), colon (transverse <italic>n</italic> = 4, sigmoid <italic>n</italic> = 4) and pancreas (<italic>n</italic> = 4). <sentence_start/>We downloaded the EPICv1 IDAT files from the ENCODE data portal<citation rid="CR127" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkz1062" pmid="31713622" pmcid="PMC7061942" count="1"><sup>127</sup></citation> and generated <italic>β</italic> values using the openSesame pipeline, as described above. <sentence_start/>We identified 159,361 CpGs that had a mean <italic>β </italic>value of <0.2 in any of the four gastrointestinal tissue types. <sentence_start/>Collectively, we selected 144,571 CpGs unmethylated in normal tissues from 12 tissue types to investigate cancer-associated DNA hypermethylation profiles (Supplementary Table 11).
TCGA-TARGET DNA methylation data

We analysed TCGA Pan-Cancer Atlas (PanCanAtlas) DNA methylation data profiled using the Infinium HumanMethylation450 (HM450) array. <sentence_start/>The raw IDAT files were obtained and processed using the R package SeSAMe. <sentence_start/>IDAT files from TARGET’s neuroblastoma and Wilms tumour projects<sup><citation rid="CR128" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.2529" pmid="23334666" pmcid="PMC3682833" count="1">128</citation>,<citation rid="CR129" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3940" pmid="28825729" pmcid="PMC5712232" count="1">129</citation></sup> were downloaded from the GDC data portal and processed using the R package SeSAMe. <sentence_start/>Our analysis included 130 Wilms tumours and 91 neuroblastomas originating in the adrenal glands.
Joint HCMI and TCGA-TARGET methylation data

We merged the HCMI and TCGA-TARGET DNA methylation data profiled using EPICv1 and HM450 arrays, respectively, to generate a dataset with the probes shared between the two platforms<citation rid="CR125" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30085201" doi="10.1093/nar/gky691" pmcid="PMC6237738" count="1"><sup>125</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>We excluded samples that had a CpG probe success rate of less than 90%. <sentence_start/>We also excluded probes with ‘NA’-masked data points that were present in more than 10% of the samples and probes on the X and Y chromosomes. <sentence_start/>To investigate the cancer-associated DNA hypermethylation profiles, we analysed the probe set that lacked tissue-specific DNA methylation (selected as described above) and then extracted 53,204 CpG sites that acquired methylation (<italic>β</italic> value of >0.3) in at least two samples in any HCMI cancer type (Supplementary Table 11).
UMAP of DNA methylation data

We performed dimension reduction using NMF on the combined HCMI and TCGA-TARGET DNA methylation data matrix described above. <sentence_start/><italic>β</italic> Values of 0 were replaced with 1.0 × 10<sup>−12</sup>, and missing values were replaced with zeros. <sentence_start/>The resulting matrix was subjected to NMF, masking zeros, as implemented in the RcppML R package (v.0.5.6)<citation rid="CR130" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2021.09.01.458620" count="1"><sup>130</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>We assessed the optimal rank for an NMF model by performing matrix decomposition across ranks ranging from 2 to 200, each with three random initializations, using the crossValidate function in the RcppML R package. <sentence_start/>We selected an NMF model of rank 170, as this model showed the minimum mean squared error of reconstruction consistently across the three runs. <sentence_start/>UMAP visualization of the rank-170 NMF model was generated using the umap function with the cosine distance metric implemented in the R package umap (v.0.2.10.0) (Supplementary Table 11). <sentence_start/>We produced the UMAP in Fig. 4c using the subset of the rank-170 NMF matrix, which included the cancer types represented in both the HCMI and the TCGA-TARGET projects.
Heatmap of DNA methylation profiles

For the four cancer cohorts on which we focused, and from the HCMI-TCGA merged DNA methylation data described above, we identified the top 10% of the most variably methylated CpGs separately in each cancer type (Fig. 4e). <sentence_start/>We selected the 8,614 CpGs that represented the union of the 4 variably methylated CpG sets. <sentence_start/>To minimize the influence of variable tumour purity levels on clustering results, we dichotomized the data, using a <italic>β</italic> value of ≥0.3 to define positive DNA methylation and <0.3 to define a lack of methylation. <sentence_start/>The sample distance matrix was computed using the Jaccard index, and then unsupervised hierarchical clustering was performed for each TMP cancer subtype. <sentence_start/>We generated the heatmap using the ComplexHeatmap R package (v.2.20.0)<citation rid="CR131" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btw313" pmid="27207943" count="1"><sup>131</sup></citation>.
Tumour-model hypermethylation similarity scores
