We assessed DNA methylation-based similarity between a model and its parent tumour based on cancer-associated CpG hypermethylation profiles. <sentence_start/>We identified the 144,571 CpGs unmethylated in normal tissues as described above. <sentence_start/>For each HCMI cancer type, we further selected CpGs hypermethylated (<italic>β</italic> value of >0.3) in at least two samples. <sentence_start/>Then we compared the Pearson’s correlation coefficient (<italic>r</italic>) as a similarity score for the following samples: (1) models and their matched tumours; (2) models and unmatched tumours from the same cancer type; and (3) models and unmatched tumours from different cancer types. <sentence_start/>A <italic>P </italic>value of paired model-tumour relatedness was then determined by calculating the probability of observing an unpaired model-tumour distance equal to or smaller than the same model’s distance to all unrelated tumours that were not from the same tissue type. <sentence_start/>After FDR adjustment, model-tumour pairs with adjusted <italic>P </italic>≥ 0.1 were considered to be models that were non-concordant with their original tumours.
Transcriptional fidelity and relatedness
RNA analyte processing and sequencing

<italic>Quality assurance and QC of RNA analytes</italic>. <sentence_start/>RNA from fresh-frozen models was sent for characterization, whereas for most tumours, samples of FFPE-derived RNA were sent. <sentence_start/>Fresh-frozen RNA analytes were assayed for RNA integrity, concentration and fragment size. <sentence_start/>Samples for total RNA-seq were quantified on a TapeStation system (Agilent) and RIN scores were calculated. <sentence_start/>Model-derived RNAs with RINs > 8.0 were considered high quality. <sentence_start/>For FFPE samples, we used DV200 and fragment size to evaluate sample quality. <sentence_start/>Although we targeted input concentrations greater than 100 ng µl<sup>-1</sup>, some FFPE samples were lower.

<italic>Total RNA-seq library construction</italic>. <sentence_start/>To construct total RNA-seq libraries, we used Illumina Stranded Total RNA Prep with RiboZero Gold, and we barcoded samples with individual tags, following the manufacturer’s instructions (Illumina). <sentence_start/>We prepared libraries, which we then pooled using an automated liquid-handling system to minimize variance. <sentence_start/>Typically, these were pools of 38-92 samples, depending on the available capacity on a sequencer. <sentence_start/>At every step we performed QC. <sentence_start/>We used a TapeStation system to quantify library concentrations, fragment size and distribution. <sentence_start/>As needed, pool balance and library quality were assessed using miSeq Nano single-end 50-bp sequencing.

<italic>Total RNA-seq</italic>. <sentence_start/>We prepared indexed libraries and ran them on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000, using paired-end 100 bp reads and generating a minimum of 150 million reads per sample library, with a target of greater than 90% mapped reads. <sentence_start/>In all but a few cases, all data were from the same sequencing run. <sentence_start/>For the few samples that needed additional read depth, we provided this with a secondary sequencing run. <sentence_start/>We demultiplexed raw Illumina sequence data and converted these to fastq files while quantifying adapter and low-quality sequences. <sentence_start/>Samples were assessed for information quality by mapping reads to the human hg38 genome reference, estimating the total number of reads that mapped, the fraction of RNA reads that mapped to coding regions, the amount of rRNA in a sample, the number of genes expressed and the relative expression of housekeeping genes. <sentence_start/>The samples that passed this quality assurance and QC step were then clustered with other expression data from similar and distinct tumour types to confirm expected expression patterns. <sentence_start/>We SNP-typed atypical samples to confirm the source analyte. <sentence_start/>FASTQ files of all reads were then uploaded to the GDC repository and distributed to the analysis teams.

<italic>MicroRNA (miRNA)-seq library construction</italic>. <sentence_start/>miRNA-seq library construction used a v4 NEXTflex Small RNA-seq kit (PerkinElmer), then samples were barcoded with individual tags following the manufacturer’s instructions. <sentence_start/>We prepared libraries on a Sciclone liquid-handling workstation. <sentence_start/>We performed QC at every step and quantified the libraries using a TapeStation system and an Agilent Bioanalyzer using a Small RNA Analysis kit. <sentence_start/>Pooled libraries were then size-selected according to specifications from a NEXTflex kit. <sentence_start/>Post-sequencing quality assurance and QC evaluated the abundance and diversity of miRNA. <sentence_start/>Data that passed were provided to the GDC.
Transcriptional relatedness measurements

<italic>MOMA subtype identification</italic>. <sentence_start/>To compare tumour subtypes in HCMI to those previously identified in TCGA, using the network-based MOMA algorithm<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2020.11.045" pmid="33434495" pmcid="PMC8103356" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation>, we used the OncoMatch algorithm<citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-22-0342" pmid="36374194" pmcid="PMC9905319" count="1"><sup>38</sup></citation> (see below). <sentence_start/>Specifically, we assessed the similarity of each HCMI sample to those in the subtypes identified by MOMA in TCGA. <sentence_start/>As these methods compare samples on the basis of the conservation of their master regulator proteins, which are highly enriched in mechanistic determinants of tumour cell state<sup><citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature08712" pmid="20032975" pmcid="PMC4011561" count="1">37</citation>,<citation rid="CR132" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0861" pmid="29510988" pmcid="PMC5967627" count="1">132</citation>-<citation rid="CR134" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-018-0138-4" pmid="29915428" pmcid="PMC6421579" count="1">134</citation></sup>, this approach effectively complements the Celligner and DNA-methylation analyses. <sentence_start/>Specifically, this analysis helps refine subtype classification by mitigating potential confounding effects in gene expression profiles-such as those related to tissue histology, unrelated to tumour biology-as well as effectively mitigating technical batch effects<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2020.11.045" pmid="33434495" pmcid="PMC8103356" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Master regulators, although rarely mutated, have crucial roles in cancer progression, as they orchestrate transcriptional networks that are disrupted by upstream genomic alterations, which makes them critical therapeutic targets<sup><citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-22-0342" pmid="36374194" pmcid="PMC9905319" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-22-1020" pmid="37061969" pmcid="PMC10239356" count="1">39</citation></sup>, including in clinical trials<sup><citation rid="CR135" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s43018-022-00489-5" pmid="36585452" pmcid="PMC9992270" count="1">135</citation>,<citation rid="CR136" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyae118" pmid="38886159" pmcid="PMC11379646" count="1">136</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>As such, they are more conserved in each tumour subtype than the corresponding transcriptional profiles<sup><citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2020.11.045" pmid="33434495" pmcid="PMC8103356" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="CR132" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0861" pmid="29510988" pmcid="PMC5967627" count="1">132</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>In the following sections, we discuss the various algorithms used in this analysis.

<italic>Original MOMA analysis</italic>. <sentence_start/>In brief, MOMA is based on the assumption that transcriptional cell states are implemented and homeostatically maintained by small, autoregulated modules of master regulator proteins, comprising transcription factors (TFs) and co-factors (co-TFs). <sentence_start/>We assessed the activities of all TFs and co-TFs using the VIPER algorithm<citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3593" pmid="27322546" pmcid="PMC5040167" count="1"><sup>137</sup></citation>, which is based on the expression of their transcriptional targets, which we inferred using the ARACNe algorithm<citation rid="CR138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng1532" pmid="15778709" count="1"><sup>138</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Tumour subtypes (<italic>n</italic> = 112) were then identified by clustering samples based on TF-co-TF activity, using the ‘partitioning around medoids’ algorithm<citation rid="CR139" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.eswa.2008.01.039" count="1"><sup>139</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Below, we describe VIPER and ARACNe.

<italic>MOMA subtype comparison</italic>. <sentence_start/>To compare HCMI samples to those in the 112 MOMA subtypes in TCGA, we first used the metaVIPER algorithm<citation rid="CR140" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-018-03843-3" pmid="29662057" pmcid="PMC5902599" count="1"><sup>140</sup></citation> to compute the activity of all TFs and co-TFs. <sentence_start/>MetaVIPER-a multinetwork version of the original VIPER algorithm<citation rid="CR137" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3593" pmid="27322546" pmcid="PMC5040167" count="1"><sup>137</sup></citation> that integrates the protein activities assessed by each network-enabled the use of networks from multiple TCGA cohorts that were matched to the histology of HCMI samples (Extended Data Table 1). <sentence_start/>Enrichment of the top 50 most differentially activated genes in a HCMI sample (that is, 25 most active and 25 most inactive) in TFs-co-TFs that were differentially expressed in each TCGA MOMA subtype were used to assess their similarity (with the OncoMatch algorithm). <sentence_start/>Indeed, we have shown that across all TCGA cohorts, >80% of the functional mutations in each sample are in pathways upstream of the top 50 master regulators. <sentence_start/>Moreover, we have shown that changing the number of master regulators between 20 and 200 does not significantly affect the OncoMatch statistics<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2020.11.045" pmid="33434495" pmcid="PMC8103356" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation>.

<italic>MetaVIPER analysis</italic>. <sentence_start/>For the analyses in this paper, we used the most recent version of the metaVIPER algorithm<citation rid="CR140" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-018-03843-3" pmid="29662057" pmcid="PMC5902599" count="1"><sup>140</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The main difference is that we replaced the original method for performing gene set analysis (aREA) by nonparametric analytical-rank-based enrichment analysis (NaRnEA)<citation rid="CR141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/e25030542" pmid="36981431" pmcid="PMC10048242" count="1"><sup>141</sup></citation>, which improved the assessment of significance for differentially active proteins. <sentence_start/>For implementing NaRnEA, we used the matrix_narnea() function in the PISCES R package<citation rid="CR142" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2021.05.20.445002" count="1"><sup>142</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>For each sample, TF-co-TF transcriptional targets (that is, regulatory networks) were inferred by ARACNe analysis of one or more lineage-matched TCGA cohorts. <sentence_start/>In brief, metaVIPER estimates the differential activity of each regulatory protein by integrating the NES statistics produced by VIPER analysis using each of the selected networks. <sentence_start/>VIPER assesses the activity of a protein by assessing the NES of its activated and repressed targets in genes that were differentially expressed in a signature of interest.

<italic>Differential expression signature generation</italic>. <sentence_start/>To remove batch effects between TCGA and HCMI samples, TPM-normalized gene expression profiles were first processed using a variational autoencoder (VAE) model called scGEN<citation rid="CR143" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41592-019-0494-8" pmid="31363220" count="1"><sup>143</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>For subtype stratification, for which the goal is to assess differentially active proteins in samples in the same cohort, differential expression signatures for VIPER analysis were optimally computed by comparing each sample to the centroid of the entire cohort. <sentence_start/>We accomplished this by subtracting the median expression across all samples and then dividing by the median absolute deviation (MAD). <sentence_start/>To prevent division by zero, MAD values <0.01 were set to 0.01. <sentence_start/>For both HCMI and TCGA, we downloaded the TPM-normalized gene expression for protein-coding transcripts from the GDC portal<citation rid="CR144" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/NEJMp1607591" pmid="27653561" pmcid="PMC6309165" count="1"><sup>144</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The cancer-specific networks used in the analysis were inferred by ARACNe as described below.

<italic>Regulatory network inference</italic>. <sentence_start/>Regulatory networks for each HCMI cohort were generated by analysing the gene expression profiles in their lineage-matched TCGA cohorts using ARACNe3 (ref. <citation rid="CR141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/e25030542" pmid="36981431" pmcid="PMC10048242" count="1"><sup>141</sup></citation>). <sentence_start/>ARACNe3 is the latest incarnation of the ARACNe algorithm<citation rid="CR138" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng1532" pmid="15778709" count="1"><sup>138</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The algorithm identifies regulatory protein-target interactions on the basis of the greatest conservation of the transferred information, as assessed by computing the mutual information on the direct path and on every indirect path traversing an intermediary TF-co-TF protein, based on the data-processing inequality<citation rid="CR145" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-2105-7-S1-S7" pmid="16723010" pmcid="PMC1810318" count="1"><sup>145</sup></citation>.

To generate cancer-type-specific networks, we applied ARACNe3 to TPM-normalized expression profiles across 32 TCGA cohorts (ACC, BLCA, BRCA, CESC, CHOL, COAD, DLBC, ESCA, GBM, HNSC, KICH, KIRC, KIRP, LGG, LIHC, LUAD, LUSC, MESO, OV, PAAD, PCPG, PRAD, READ, SARC, SKCM, STAD, TGCT, THCA, THYM, UCEC, UCS and UVM). <sentence_start/>Each ARACNe3 network was inferred by subsampling the gene expression profiles until ≥50 targets were identified for each TF-co-TF in the consensus network. <sentence_start/>The analysis included 1,645 TFs and 1,556 co-TFs, retrieved from ref. <citation rid="CR146" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2018.01.029" pmid="29425488" pmcid="PMC12908702" count="1"><sup>146</sup></citation> and ref. <citation rid="CR147" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/nar/gkw1007" pmid="27789689" pmcid="PMC5210517" count="1"><sup>147</sup></citation>, respectively. <sentence_start/>Networks were pruned to the 100 most significant targets for each regulatory protein, based on consensus mutual information statistics. <sentence_start/>For TCGA-ESCA, we inferred networks for adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, separately.

<italic>OncoMatch analysis</italic>. <sentence_start/>OncoMatch<citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-22-0342" pmid="36374194" pmcid="PMC9905319" count="1"><sup>38</sup></citation> was used to assess the similarity between HCMI and TCGA samples based on a weighted enrichment analysis of their differential protein activities. <sentence_start/>First, we computed the differential protein activities for each of <italic>n</italic> = 112 MOMA subtypes, as assessed by analysis of 20 cohorts with sufficient size for the analysis, including BLCA, BRCA, COAD, GBM, HNSC, KIRC, LAML, LGG, LIHC, LUAD, LUSC, OV, PAAD, PRAD, READ, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA and UCEC. <sentence_start/>Specifically, for each subtype, we generated an average protein activity (consensus protein activity signature) by integrating its VIPER-inferred NES values across each sample in the subtype, using Stouffer’s <italic>z</italic> score method. <sentence_start/>Then, we generated a <italic>P </italic>value to assess the similarity of each HCMI sample to each MOMA subtype in its lineage-matched cohorts. <sentence_start/>This was accomplished by assessing the following criteria: (1) the enrichment of the top 50 most differentially active protein (top and bottom 25) in the HCMI sample in a protein differentially active in the consensus protein activity signature of each MOMA subtype using NaRnEA; (2) the enrichment of the top 50 most differentially active protein (top and bottom 25) in the consensus protein activity signature of each MOMA subtype in a protein differentially active in the HCMI sample; and (3) by integrating the two using Stouffer’s method.

HCMI samples may show high similarity to more than one subtype. <sentence_start/>As such, a final assignment was performed as follows. <sentence_start/>As the tumour and the model samples were derived from the same tumour mass, we assumed that their subtype assignment should be conserved. <sentence_start/>Thus, among all MOMA subtypes producing a significant match to a model and its parental tumour <italic>P</italic> < 0.05, one-tailed, Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted, we selected the subtype with their best integrated Stouffer score. <sentence_start/>If no agreement was identified (that is, no MOMA subtype with significant OncoMatch score for both the model and its parental tumour), then the two were independently assigned to their best scoring MOMA subtype. <sentence_start/>For simplicity, we mapped HCMI colorectal, oesophageal-gastric and GBM samples only to COAD, STAD and GBM MOMA subtypes in TCGA, respectively, thus excluding subtypes from READ, ESCA and LGG. <sentence_start/>A null model for the OncoMatch analysis was generated by generating a probability density of OncoMatch NES scores matching each HCMI sample to all non-lineage-related TCGA subtypes. <sentence_start/>A one-tail <italic>P </italic>value was assessed, as the only relevant result would be for the HCMI OncoMatch score to be larger than the OncoMatch from the null hypothesis.

<italic>Tumour-model similarity analysis</italic>. <sentence_start/>The transcriptional state similarity between models and their parental tumours was also assessed based on OncoMatch statistics. <sentence_start/>Differential expression signatures for VIPER analysis were computed by further normalizing and scaling the TPM-normalized gene expression data by subtracting the median expression across all same type samples (that is, tumours or models) in the same HCMI cohort and dividing by the MAD. <sentence_start/>Again, to prevent division by zero, MAD values <0.01 were set to 0.01. <sentence_start/>Differential gene expression was assessed separately for tumours and models to avoid sample type related batch effects. <sentence_start/>For small cohorts (<italic>n</italic> ≤ 10 samples), we used the median and the MAD of lineage-matched samples that they belonged to. <sentence_start/>Specifically, the following cohorts were normalized together: (1) intrahepatic, extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma; (2) all sarcoma types, including bone cancer and desmoid tumours; and (3) tubulovillous adenoma, rare gastrointestinal cancers and colorectal cancer. <sentence_start/>Similar to the above analysis, we inferred protein activity using metaVIPER with the NaRnEA enrichment analysis algorithm and cancer-type-specific networks. <sentence_start/>For instance, some HCMI cohorts (for example, COAD) could be matched to multiple lineage networks inferred from TCGA cohorts (that is, COAD and READ). <sentence_start/>Thus, we assessed protein activities for colorectal, lung, bile duct-liver, brain and gastroesophageal samples in HCMI using COAD-READ, LUAD-LUSC, LIHC-CHOL, GBM-LGG and ESCA-STAD networks, respectively. <sentence_start/>For rare cohorts that lacked sufficient samples to perform ARACNe analyses, (that is, Wilms tumour, small intestine cancer, gallbladder cancer and unknown carcinoma), we leveraged the ability of metaVIPER to automatically integrate across multiple networks. <sentence_start/>Specifically, we selected the three networks that produced the greatest differential activity for the top 50 proteins. <sentence_start/>The rationale is that incorrect networks can only decrease but not increase activity (that is, the more unrelated the network, the smaller the differential activity). <sentence_start/>To avoid diluting the results based on subpar networks, networks that produced significantly lower differential activity for each protein were excluded from the analysis. <sentence_start/>We also normalized samples in rare cohorts together with the samples identified as having the best matching networks.

To generate a conservative, nonparametric null-model, we computed the probability density function (PDF) of the NES generated by matching each model with all the non-lineage-matched tumours in HCMI. <sentence_start/>To improve the PDF estimate, which was highly non-Gaussian, we bootstrapped null-model generation 1,000 times using 60% of the non-lineage-matched samples and used the resulting PDF to convert matched tumour-model pair values to <italic>z</italic> scores. <sentence_start/>As both positive and negative NES were integrated, we used Stouffer’s method to generate integrated <italic>z</italic> scores. <sentence_start/>Tumour-model pairs with FDR > 0.1 were considered poor matches.

<italic>Celligner</italic>. <sentence_start/>To align our HCMI collection to publicly available collections of tumours (TCGA and TARGET) and models (CCLE), we used Celligner<citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-20294-x" pmid="33397959" pmcid="PMC7782593" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation>, a computational framework to integrate and compare multiple gene expression datasets. <sentence_start/>Initially, we attempted to expand the tumour and model datasets by directly merging the transcriptional profile of the HCMI collection. <sentence_start/>However, this approach resulted in poor alignment of the data (Supplementary Fig. 10a). <sentence_start/>To address this, we expanded on the established Celligner approach by aligning the HCMI dataset to the existing reference datasets in a two-step process. <sentence_start/>First, we replicated the alignment of TCGA and TARGET tumours onto the CCLE cell lines to create a reference tumour-model map, as described in the original Celligner publication<citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-20294-x" pmid="33397959" pmcid="PMC7782593" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation> . <sentence_start/>Subsequently, we introduced the HCMI dataset into this integrated space.

In brief, using contrastive PCA, we identified gene expression signatures elevated in the TCGA-TARGET tumour collection compared with the CCLE models, consistent with the results reported in the original Celligner analysis (Supplementary Fig. 10b). <sentence_start/>These signatures were enriched for pathways related to immune and non-malignant features, including stromal cell enrichment (Supplementary Fig. 10b). <sentence_start/>To mitigate the influence of these non-malignant features, we removed the contrastive principal components (cPCs) associated with these signatures before proceeding to the next steps. <sentence_start/>We then applied mutual nearest neighbours (MNN) batch correction as part of the Celligner algorithm to align the datasets.

Using this aligned gene expression space as a reference, we integrated the HCMI models and tumours. <sentence_start/>Specifically, we removed the cPCs increased in the HCMI dataset, which were similarly enriched for immune-related gene signatures (Supplementary Fig. 10c), correlated to DNA-based tumour impurity assessment (Supplementary Fig. 10d) and then we applied MNN batch correction. <sentence_start/>For this integration, we removed the first three cPCs, which maximized the number of MNN pairs (Supplementary Fig. 10e) and aligned well with the expected variability in the dataset through gene-set enrichment analysis of gene expression profiles. <sentence_start/>We used a <italic>k</italic><sub>1</sub> value of 20 and <italic>k</italic><sub>2</sub> value of 50 for MNN, as recommended by the Celligner developers, to reflect differences in dataset size and composition. <sentence_start/>The results suggested that the HCMI tumour collection exhibited similar levels of variability and contamination as the reference TCGA-TARGET dataset.

After integrating all datasets, we performed PCA on the combined data and calculated pairwise Euclidean distances between all tumours and models in the 70-PC space. <sentence_start/>These distances formed the basis for all Celligner distance-based analyses that we described in this study. <sentence_start/>To visualize the integrated data, we created a 2D UMAP embedding based on the 70 PCs for visualization (Supplementary Table 11).

To measure transcriptional relatedness between matched HCMI model-tumour pairs, we used the Celligner distances, which represent the Euclidean distance between a model and its paired tumour in 70-PC space. <sentence_start/>A <italic>P</italic> value of paired model-tumour relatedness was then determined by calculating the probability that an unpaired model-tumour distance equal to or smaller than the same model’s distance to all unrelated tumours that were not from the same tissue type. <sentence_start/>After FDR adjustment, model-tumour pairs with adjusted <italic>P </italic>values equal to or greater than 0.1 were considered to be models that were non-concordant with their original tumours. <sentence_start/>Relatedness of tumour lineage is as indicated in Supplementary Table 12.

<italic>Expression data input for Celligner</italic>. <sentence_start/>TARGET samples (<italic>n</italic> = 784) and TCGA expression data (<italic>n</italic> = 9,806) were obtained from the Xena browser ( ). <sentence_start/>Cell line gene expression data for 1,377 samples were taken from the DepMap Public 19Q4 file. <sentence_start/>HCMI dataset expression data were downloaded from the GDC portal, and TPM unstranded data were used for only protein-coding genes. <sentence_start/>Gene expression data were then log<sub>2</sub> transformed after adding a pseudocount of 1. <sentence_start/>Finally, we subset gene expression data to the 18,550 protein-coding genes that were present in all datasets for all Celligner analyses.

<italic>Euclidean and latent TF (OHSU methods) preprocessing</italic>. <sentence_start/>The unique genetic and molecular distribution call for each cancer cohort (for example, pancreatic cancer) and specimen type (that is, tumour or derived model) for these groupings suggested that each be run independently through the following pipeline. <sentence_start/>We filtered RNA gene expression data for biologically relevant features (the combined set of feature-selected genes of top methods from TCGA trained algorithms)<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2024.12.002" pmid="39753139" pmcid="PMC11949768" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>For instances where it was needed for analysis, we aggregated multiple TCGA cohorts to more closely match the specific cancer types included in HCMI cohorts (that is, the HCMI lung cancer cohort included TCGA LUAD and LUSC cohorts; the HCMI STAD-ESCC cohort included TCGA GEA and ESCC cohorts; the HCMI kidney cohort included KIRP, KIRC and KICH TCGA cohorts). <sentence_start/>Any remaining cohorts with low sample size (<italic>n</italic> < 8) were statistically underpowered and excluded from downstream analysis.

<italic>Euclidean distance calculation</italic>. <sentence_start/>Euclidean-based distances were measured in a group (for example, in pancreatic tumours). <sentence_start/>First, we computed the mean pairwise gene Euclidean distances. <sentence_start/>For example, we generated a list of pairwise gene distances by calculating all gene distances between pairs of samples. <sentence_start/>We reported the sample pair distance as the mean of this list. <sentence_start/>We then repeated the process for all sample pairs, reporting sample pairs for both tumour-tumour pairs for intracohort similarity and tumour-model matched pairs for derived model similarity. <sentence_start/>We report the <italic>z</italic> score of these distances and identified outliers as (>3 <italic>z</italic> score).

Latent TF distance calculation. <sentence_start/>Latent TF distances were generated using neural networks. <sentence_start/>Specifically, a variational autoencoder model (NetVae) was trained with gene expression of normal tissues from all TCGA cohorts and genotype-tissue expression (GTEx). <sentence_start/>These datasets were aligned using quantile ranking. <sentence_start/>On a gene-wise basis, we calculated the summed difference between a HCMI sample (tumour or model) and normal tissue. <sentence_start/>These deviation scores were then correlated with mutations and encoded into latent space. <sentence_start/>The same methods described in the section ‘Euclidean distance calculation’ were applied to these latent values to generate the latent TF distances. <sentence_start/>Both intracohort and intercohort distances were calculated.

<italic>Multiclass pair classification-based distance calculation</italic>. <sentence_start/>We observed that relative gene expression was effective in removing batch effects across different datasets. <sentence_start/>When we plotted TCGA data using the relative expression of the most variable 500 genes on UMAP space and mapped HCMI samples to the plot, we found that data were clustered on the basis of tissue type. <sentence_start/>This was in contrast to continuous gene expression data, which clustered data in cohorts. <sentence_start/>Given this, we used a multiclass pair classification-based approach to compute the distances between matched tumour-model pairs. <sentence_start/>The multiclass pair classification algorithm<citation rid="CR148" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btab088" pmid="33543757" pmcid="PMC8479681" count="1"><sup>148</sup></citation> uses the relative expression between gene pairs as input and is an extension to multiple classes of the <italic>k</italic>-top-scoring pairs algorithm<citation rid="CR149" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btu622" pmid="25262153" pmcid="PMC4287945" count="1"><sup>149</sup></citation> that was developed for binary classification. <sentence_start/>We regressed out the purity effects in both TMP and HCMI data and found that removing purity effects did not make subtypes indistinguishable. <sentence_start/>We applied the best model selected over cross validations in TMP data to HCMI models and tumours and computed the pairwise Euclidean distances between the assignment probabilities of each HCMI sample to TMP cohort subtypes. <sentence_start/>We labelled a matched tumour-model distance as an outlier if it was above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR of the tumour-model distances in the TMP cohort.

<italic>Canonical parallel direction</italic>. <sentence_start/>We transformed and normalized the combined gene expression matrix using the variance-stabilizing transform from DESeq2 (ref. <citation rid="CR150" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8" pmid="25516281" pmcid="PMC4302049" count="1"><sup>150</sup></citation>) then split the matrix into separate tumour and model matrices. <sentence_start/>We calculated the canonical parallel direction (CPD) by taking the difference between tumour-model pairs and then performing PCA on the resulting difference matrix with the R package irlba ( ). <sentence_start/>We took the CPD as the first loading vector. <sentence_start/>We derived distances by projecting individual expression matrices onto the CPD to obtain a score, and we took the difference in scores between model-tumour pairs as the CPD distance. <sentence_start/>We labelled samples as outliers when their distance was greater than two standard deviations from the mean.
HCMI and CCLE model coverage comparison

A critical rationale for model generation is to provide proxies for in vitro or in vivo studies of tumour biology. <sentence_start/>As a result, it is critical to assess what fraction of the tumours in a large-scale repository (for example, TCGA) are associated with effective proxies in large model repositories such as CCLE and HCMI. <sentence_start/>For this purpose, we assessed the fraction of TCGA tumours that had at least one high-fidelity matched model in CCLE and HCMI. <sentence_start/>Specifically, we identified high-fidelity models as those producing an OncoMatch score of NES ≥ 10, as previously discussed<sup><citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-22-0342" pmid="36374194" pmcid="PMC9905319" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/2159-8290.CD-22-1020" pmid="37061969" pmcid="PMC10239356" count="1">39</citation></sup>.

For this purpose, we generated violin plots representing the probability density of the highest OncoMatch NES scores against each model in HCMI, CCLE and the joint repository of HCMI and CCLE models. <sentence_start/>As in the other analyses, batch-effect-corrected, TPM-normalized datasets were mitigated using the scGEN algorithm, without considering cancer type and tumour-model covariates. <sentence_start/>Then, TPM-normalized CCLE gene expression profiles were obtained from DepMap 21Q3 (refs. <sup><citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2017.06.010" pmid="28753430" pmcid="PMC5667678" count="1">9</citation>,<citation rid="CR151" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.6084/m9.figshare.15160110.v3" count="1">151</citation></sup>). <sentence_start/>Gene expression profiles were then centred by subtracting the median expression across all samples and dividing by the MAD. <sentence_start/>As discussed in previous sections, we used MetaVIPER to assess the activity of TF and co-TF proteins, using regulatory networks generated by ARACNe analysis of the TCGA cohort from which each tumour sample was selected.
Tumour molecular pathology subtype predictions

We predicted the subtype of each sample using TMP models<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2024.12.002" pmid="39753139" pmcid="PMC11949768" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>These models were trained on molecular data (gene expression, CNV, DNA methylation, miRNA expression and somatic mutations) from TCGA primary tumours. <sentence_start/>We included a library of models that used either one data type or multiple data types. <sentence_start/>We applied models that used only gene expression, or DNA methylation, to HCMI samples because of their top performance with TCGA data. <sentence_start/>We quantile-ranked gene expression data before application. <sentence_start/>For each sample, we report a single subtype by considering all models and their model confidence values (for example, we report the consensus subtype of the five independent models that were run for ovarian samples).
snRNA-seq analysis
snRNA-seq sample preparation and analysis

Frozen samples (<italic>n</italic> = 34, from 17 tumour-model pairs) were obtained from the BPC Nationwide Children’s Hospital, DFCI and ATCC. <sentence_start/>Nucleus isolation was performed using a Chromium Nuclei Isolation kit with RNase inhibitor (10x Genomics, 1000494). <sentence_start/>Samples were homogenized using a pestle in lysis buffer, passed through a column and centrifuged in debris-removal buffer to eliminate residual tissue and debris. <sentence_start/>The isolated nuclei were then washed, resuspended and loaded onto a 10x Chromium platform for gel bead-in-emulsion (GEM) generation and barcoding. <sentence_start/>Following GEM reverse transcription, samples underwent post-GEM RT cleanup and cDNA amplification. <sentence_start/>After quality control and quantification of cDNA, libraries were prepared using the Chromium Single Cell 3′ Gene Expression Library Construction protocol and sequenced on a NovaSeq platform.

We aligned snRNA-seq short-read data from 17 tumour-model pairs (34 samples) multiplexed across 16 runs, generated by the Columbia University Single Cell Analysis Core, including 7 GBM, 6 PAAD and 4 COAD pairs, to the prebuilt 10x Genomics human reference genome GRCh38-2024-A, using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger software (v.8.0.1)<citation rid="CR152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms14049" pmid="28091601" pmcid="PMC5241818" count="1"><sup>152</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Illumina base call files were converted to FASTQ files with the command cellranger mkfastq. <sentence_start/>Expression data were processed with cellranger count on the pre-built human reference, which encompassed 38,606 features. <sentence_start/>Cell Ranger performsd default filtering for QC, and generates filtered feature-barcode matrix files (filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5; barcodes.tsv, genes.tsv, and matrix.mts) containing unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts for genes for each run.
snRNA-seq demultiplexing

To recover sample-specific profiles for samples processed in the same 10x Chromium flow cell, we demultiplexed the Cell Ranger output<citation rid="CR152" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ncomms14049" pmid="28091601" pmcid="PMC5241818" count="1"><sup>152</sup></citation> using Demuxlet<citation rid="CR153" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nbt.4042" pmid="29227470" pmcid="PMC5784859" count="1"><sup>153</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>As Demuxlet requires a list of sample-specific SNPs as an input, we called germline variants for each human sample from the matched normal WGS data. <sentence_start/>To limit the number of false-positive doublets, which are common in snRNA-seq demultiplexing owing to background RNA and potential large duplications or deletions shared by tumours in the same cohort, we used the gnomADv4 exome data to subset only the most likely germline variants. <sentence_start/>Specifically, we retained only biallelic SNPs that met the following criteria: (1) population MAF ≥ 0.1%; (2) identified in the gnomADv4 WES cohort<citation rid="CR154" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-023-06045-0" pmid="38057664" pmcid="PMC11629659" count="1"><sup>154</sup></citation>; and (3) flagged as PASS in gnomAD. <sentence_start/>We ran Demuxlet with the following parameters: --field GT and --group-list barcodes.txt, where ‘barcodes.txt’ was the cell barcode file generated by Cell Ranger. <sentence_start/>As previously recommended<citation rid="CR155" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-019-10756-2" pmid="31266958" pmcid="PMC6606589" count="1"><sup>155</sup></citation> for demultiplexing snRNA-seq samples, we assigned cells to a sample and used these cells in downstream analyses only if the BEST column of the Demuxlet-generated <Cell Ranger run >.best file started with ‘SNG-’ or the BEST column started with ‘DBL-’ and the PRB.DBL column contained a value of ≤0.99. <sentence_start/>We classified droplet barcodes with ‘DBL-’ in the BEST column and >0.99 in the PRB.DBL column as doublets, whereas those labelled with AMB were unassigned; droplets labelled as doublet or unassigned were excluded from downstream analyses.
snRNA-seq gene expression analysis

UMI matrices for each demultiplexed sample were processed using Scanpy (v.1.9.3)<citation rid="CR156" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13059-017-1382-0" pmid="29409532" pmcid="PMC5802054" count="1"><sup>156</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>For QC, we only retained cells with <25% mitochondrial RNA content and UMI counts in the range (800; 50,000). <sentence_start/>To recover more cells in tumour samples with low cell counts (that is, cases HCM-BROD-0110-C25 and HCM-CSHL-0073-C25), we increased the mitochondrial RNA content threshold to 35% and removed the lower bound on UMI counts. <sentence_start/>To recover more cells from a run that included three COAD tumours, we removed the threshold on mitochondrial RNA content while maintaining an upper UMI count limit of 100,000. <sentence_start/>Owing to the low number of cells in the tumour from case HCM-CSHL-0247-C18, we excluded this tumour-model pair from downstream analyses. <sentence_start/>As a result, we analysed 16 tumour-model pairs: 7 for GBM, 6 for PAAD and 3 for COAD. <sentence_start/>For statistics on UMI counts before and after QC for individual samples, refer to Supplementary Table 8. <sentence_start/>UMI counts were normalized, log transformed and scaled, following the standard Scanpy preprocessing workflow. <sentence_start/>PCA was performed with the ‘arpack’ solver (‘scanpy.tl.pca’). <sentence_start/>The nearest-neighbour distance matrix was computed with ‘scanpy.pp.neighbors’, setting ‘n_neighbors’ = 15 (default). <sentence_start/>UMAP embeddings were computed using ‘scanpy.tl.umap’, and PCA and UMAP visualizations were generated with the ‘scanpy.pl.pca’ and ‘scanpy.pl.umap’ functions. <sentence_start/>For analyses involving dimensionality reduction and visualization of tumour-model pairs or involving multiple cases, the same single-sample workflow was applied by re-scaling the multi-sample concatenated data. <sentence_start/>Individual samples were clustered using the resolution-optimized Leiden clustering algorithm via the acdc-py wrapper for the Scanpy’s Leiden implementation ( ). <sentence_start/>We determined the optimal number of clusters by varying resolution values from 0.01 to 1.01 in 0.01 increments, selecting the solution that produced the highest average Silhouette score.
Copy number and putative malignant cells detection

We inferred CNAs from expression counts at the single-nucleus level using the inferCNV package<citation rid="CR157" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>157</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>We clustered nuclei according to their unsupervised clustering labels, based on gene expression. <sentence_start/>A reference set of 2,193 nuclei (1,840 oligodendrocytes and 352 microglia) were sampled from four GBM tumours (HCM-BROD-0199-C71, HCM-BROD-0415-C71, HCM-BROD-0012-C71 and HCM-BROD-0002-C71). <sentence_start/>We used these reference nuclei as controls to infer CNAs in GBM samples. <sentence_start/>We used a reference set of 3,592 nuclei (2,112 fibroblasts and 1,480 stellate cells) sampled from 6 PAAD tumours (HCM-CSHL-0078-C25 primary and metastatic, HCM-CSHL-0089-C25 primary and metastatic, HCM-CSHL-0073-C25 and HCM-BROD-0110-C25) to infer CNAs in each PAAD sample. <sentence_start/>We labelled cell types in the references (oligodendrocytes, microglia, fibroblasts and stellate cells) via over-representation analysis (ORA) using the Python decoupler package with canonical human markers (‘brain’ and ‘immune system’ for GBMs; ‘pancreas’, ‘immune system’ and ‘connective tissue’ for PAAD) from the PanglaoDB database<sup><citation rid="CR158" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioadv/vbac016" pmid="36699385" pmcid="PMC9710656" count="1">158</citation>,<citation rid="CR159" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/database/baz046" pmid="30951143" pmcid="PMC6450036" count="1">159</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>We sampled a reference set of 435 nuclei (annotated as macrophages by SingleR) sampled from HCM-BROD-0001-C18, and we used the only COAD sample that had enough non-epithelial cells to infer CNAs in each COAD sample. <sentence_start/>The following parameters were used in each inferCNV run: cutoff=0.1, window_length = 101, HMM=TRUE, mode=’i6’, analysis_mode = ‘subclusters’, denoise=TRUE. <sentence_start/>To classify putative malignant cells, we compared the inferred CNAs in each snRNA-seq sample to the CNAs detected by WGS in matched bulk samples. <sentence_start/>Cells were labelled as malignant if they belonged to a cluster with those CNAs.
Cell-type calling for GBM samples

snRNA-seq profiles from GBM samples first underwent coarse-grain cell-type assignment via ORA, using the decoupler Python package with canonical human markers for the brain from the PanglaoDB database<sup><citation rid="CR158" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioadv/vbac016" pmid="36699385" pmcid="PMC9710656" count="1">158</citation>,<citation rid="CR159" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/database/baz046" pmid="30951143" pmcid="PMC6450036" count="1">159</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>To address the low signal-to-noise ratio inherent in snRNA-seq data, we performed soft gene imputation by summing the UMI counts of the ten nearest neighbours of each nucleus before running ORA. <sentence_start/>We labelled nuclei not labelled as ‘oligodendrocytes’ or ‘microglia’ and belonging to clusters of putative malignant cells from inferCNV analysis as ‘malignant’ and assigned these cells to specific cellular states, as described below.
Malignant state assignment for GBM samples

For each GBM nucleus labelled as malignant, a gene expression signature was computed as follows: , where is the <italic>d</italic>-dimensional vector of ln(<italic>x</italic> + 1)-transformed gene expression for nucleus <italic>i</italic> in snRNA-seq sample <italic>k</italic> (with <italic>d</italic> equal to the number of genes), and and are the <italic>d</italic>-dimensional vectors representing the mean and standard deviation of ln(<italic>x</italic> + 1)-transformed gene expression across all malignant GBM snRNA-seq profiles, respectively. <sentence_start/>We performed gene set enrichment analysis of each gene expression signature across the six subtypes-NPC1-like, NPC2-like, MES1-like, MES2-like AC-like and OPC-like-as previously identified<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2019.06.024" pmid="31327527" pmcid="PMC6703186" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation>, using the NaRnEA algorithm<citation rid="CR141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/e25030542" pmid="36981431" pmcid="PMC10048242" count="1"><sup>141</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>For this purpose, we used the Python package ‘pyVIPER’<citation rid="CR160" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12859-026-06524-x" pmcid="PMC13471495" pmid="42332576" count="1"><sup>160</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Each gene set comprised 39-50 genes that represented distinct cellular states. <sentence_start/>We then assigned each nucleus to the subtype that produced the maximum NaRnEA NES. <sentence_start/>Nuclei with the smallest <italic>P</italic> value (>0.15) were assigned no cellular state and were labelled as unknown. <sentence_start/>For simplicity, we combined the NPC1-like and NPC2-like subtypes into a single NPC-like subtype; similarly, we merged the MES1-like and MES-2 like subtypes into a single MES-like subtype.
Cell-type calling for PAAD and COAD samples

For each PAAD and COAD snRNA-seq profile, an initial coarse-grain cell-type assignment was performed using the Python implementation of SingleR using the Blueprint-ENCODE reference<sup><citation rid="CR161" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3324/haematol.2013.094243" pmid="24091925" pmcid="PMC3789449" count="1">161</citation>,<citation rid="CR162" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature11247" pmid="22955616" pmcid="PMC3439153" count="1">162</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>SingleR computes the correlation between each individual nucleus and every sample in the reference. <sentence_start/>It then labels each nucleus with the cell type with the highest average correlation. <sentence_start/>To deal with the low signal-to-noise ratio characteristic of snRNA-seq data, before to running SingleR, we applied soft gene imputation using a metacell approach. <sentence_start/>That is, by adding the UMI counts of the ten nearest neighbours of each nucleus using scanpy.pp.neighbors (Euclidean distance). <sentence_start/>Nuclei with an ‘epithelial cell’ annotation, which were also classified as putative malignant cells on the basis of inferCNV analysis, were labelled as malignant and assigned to specific transcriptional states, as detailed below. <sentence_start/>In the COAD cohort, we also retained a small subset of putative malignant cells annotated as ‘neurons’ by SingleR, as these were likely to be malignant cells with neuroendocrine features.
Malignant state assignment for PAAD samples

For nuclei derived from PAAD samples, we used a subtype classification strategy similar to that for GBM. <sentence_start/>We tested three classification strategies proposed in the literature, including those proposed by ref. <citation rid="CR163" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3398" pmid="26343385" pmcid="PMC4912058" count="1"><sup>163</sup></citation>, ref. <citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2021.11.017" pmid="34890551" pmcid="PMC8822455" count="1"><sup>34</sup></citation> ref. <citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2020.10.27.357269" pmcid="PMC13553295" pmid="42649389" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation>; the first was from bulk profiles and the other were two from single-cell profiles. <sentence_start/>For the first two, we used the same methodology described for the GBM samples. <sentence_start/>For the latter, we performed the comparison at the protein activity level. <sentence_start/>Specifically, protein activity in malignant cells was assessed using metaVIPER<citation rid="CR140" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-018-03843-3" pmid="29662057" pmcid="PMC5902599" count="1"><sup>140</sup></citation> by integrating six PAAD gene regulatory networks, which we generated independently from distinct PAAD cohorts, including single-cell profiles (scNET)<citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2020.10.27.357269" pmcid="PMC13553295" pmid="42649389" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation>, laser microdissected samples (CUMC-net)<citation rid="CR164" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/gutjnl-2018-317706" pmid="30658994" pmcid="PMC6509007" count="1"><sup>164</sup></citation>, the TCGA PAAD cohort (TCGA-net)<citation rid="CR165" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2017.07.007" pmid="28810144" pmcid="PMC5964983" count="1"><sup>165</sup></citation>, the ICGC PAAD cohort (ICGC-net)<citation rid="CR166" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature16965" pmid="26909576" count="1"><sup>166</sup></citation>, the UNC cohort (UNC-net)<citation rid="CR163" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ng.3398" pmid="26343385" pmcid="PMC4912058" count="1"><sup>163</sup></citation> and single-cell profiles from HCMI samples (HCMI-net). <sentence_start/>These networks captured regulatory interactions for TFs, co-TFs, signalling proteins and surface markers. <sentence_start/>For the first five networks, detailed information for the generation has been previously provided<citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2020.10.27.357269" pmcid="PMC13553295" pmid="42649389" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The HCMI-net was generated from snRNA-seq profiles from malignant nuclei in the HCMI PAAD cohort using ARACNe3 (ref. <citation rid="CR141" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/e25030542" pmid="36981431" pmcid="PMC10048242" count="1"><sup>141</sup></citation>), with metacell generation constructed using the ‘pyviper.pp.repr_metacells’ function as input (the metacell approach adaptively aims at a target median depth of 10,000 UMIs per metacell whenever feasible). <sentence_start/>Although this target was not always met, a minimum depth of 8,432 UMIs was reached, which ensured robust representation of the gene expression profiles. <sentence_start/>To avoid bias associated with different regulon size, all regulons were pruned to the 100 most significant targets based on mutual information analysis. <sentence_start/>We then classified each single cell on the basis of three main PAAD transcriptional lineages identified as previously described<citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2020.10.27.357269" pmcid="PMC13553295" pmid="42649389" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation>, including GLS, MOS and PLS. <sentence_start/>Classification was based on the significance of the NaRnEA-based NES representing the enrichment of the top 100 most differentially active proteins in each single nucleus (50 most activated and 50 most inactivated proteins) differentially active in the GLS, MOS and PLS signatures. <sentence_start/>Each nucleus was assigned to the cell state with the highest NaRnEA-inferred NES. <sentence_start/>Nuclei in which the highest-scoring subtype had a <italic>P </italic>> 0.15 were assigned to no specific transcriptional state and were labelled as ‘unknown’.
Malignant state assignment for COAD samples

For each nucleus in the COAD cohort, we computed a gene expression signature using the same methodology as applied to GBM and PAAD samples. <sentence_start/>Enrichment of each signature for two previously reported intrinsic subtypes, iCMS2 and iCMS3 (ref. <citation rid="CR167" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-022-01100-4" pmid="35773407" pmcid="PMC9279158" count="1"><sup>167</sup></citation>), was calculated using NaRnEA based on the 50 most overexpressed and 50 most underexpressed genes in each signature. <sentence_start/>Each nucleus was assigned to the cellular state corresponding to the highest NES, whereas nuclei with a <italic>P</italic> >0.15 value were labelled as unknown. <sentence_start/>The vast majority of cells in HCM-CSHL-0143-C20 and HCM-CSHL-0322-C20 were classified as iCMS2, the predominant epithelial state, which is enriched in tumours with strong WNT and MYC signalling activation<sup><citation rid="CR167" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-022-01100-4" pmid="35773407" pmcid="PMC9279158" count="1">167</citation>,<citation rid="CR168" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3967" pmid="26457759" pmcid="PMC4636487" count="1">168</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>We identified a subset of iCMS3 cells, typically in tumours with substantial immune activation and metabolic dysregulation<sup><citation rid="CR167" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41588-022-01100-4" pmid="35773407" pmcid="PMC9279158" count="1">167</citation>,<citation rid="CR168" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nm.3967" pmid="26457759" pmcid="PMC4636487" count="1">168</citation></sup>, in the HCM-BROD-0001-C18 tumour-model pair (about 50% in the tumour, around 20% in the model; Extended Data Fig. 8b,c). <sentence_start/>Although the proportions of iCMS2 and iCMS3 cells differed between the tumour and model, the analysis demonstrated that the model effectively recapitulated both cell states that were observed in the parental tumour.
Tumour-model differential gene expression

Differentially expressed genes between tumour and matched model samples were called using the Scanpy function ‘scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups’ after ln(<italic>x </italic>+ 1) transformation. <sentence_start/>Statistics were assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test followed by Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple-hypothesis testing. <sentence_start/>We used the resulting signatures to assess pathway enrichment with the ‘pyviper.tl.path_enr’ function in pyVIPER<citation rid="CR160" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12859-026-06524-x" pmcid="PMC13471495" pmid="42332576" count="1"><sup>160</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The following gene sets were used: MSigDB Hallmark gene sets for PAAD and COAD<citation rid="CR169" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cels.2015.12.004" pmid="26771021" pmcid="PMC4707969" count="1"><sup>169</sup></citation>; MSigDB Hallmark gene sets<citation rid="CR169" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cels.2015.12.004" pmid="26771021" pmcid="PMC4707969" count="1"><sup>169</sup></citation>; single-cell GBM expression meta-modules<citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2019.06.024" pmid="31327527" pmcid="PMC6703186" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation>; and bulk-based transcriptional signatures<citation rid="CR170" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ccell.2017.06.003" pmid="28697342" pmcid="PMC5599156" count="1"><sup>170</sup></citation> for GBM cases.
Medium-switching assay

To assess transcriptional plasticity driven by culture media, HCM-BROD-0416-C71 GBM cells, originally maintained in NSA medium, were transitioned to formulated-conditioned medium. <sentence_start/>After initial recovery and expansion in NSA medium, cells were plated on laminin-coated culture vessels and, following 24 h of adhesion, switched to formulated-conditioned medium for either 72 h or 2 weeks. <sentence_start/>Cells were then fixed and stained for the indicated markers and imaged using the Operetta CLS High-Content Analysis system (Revvity). <sentence_start/>Full experimental details are provided in the Supplementary Methods.
In vitro drug-sensitivity testing

Patient-derived GBM cells were maintained in NSA medium supplemented with epidermal growth factor and fibroblast growth factor under standard culture conditions<sup><citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-11-3084" pmid="22316604" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="CR51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-2209-9" pmid="32322066" pmcid="PMC8235024" count="1">51</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>For drug-sensitivity assays, cells were seeded at a density of 2,000 cells per well in ultra-low-attachment 96-well plates. <sentence_start/>Twenty-four hours after seeding, temozolomide was dispensed using a D300e digital dispenser in an 8-point titration series (0.03-300 µM). <sentence_start/>Cell viability was assessed after 5 days using a CellTiter-Glo luminescent assay (Promega).
The HCMI Explorer Suite

To facilitate the exploration of HCMI translational and clinical utility, we developed the HCMI Explorer Suite, a web-based application built using R Shiny (v.1.8.1.1)<citation rid="CR171" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>171</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The application was developed in the R programming language (v.4.3.2) and leverages key Shiny packages such as shiny, shinydashboard and shinythemes to provide a dynamic and interactive graphical user interface. <sentence_start/>The core modules of the HCMI Explorer Suite enable users to explore treatment timelines, model-specific genomic data and transcriptional similarities between cancer models, paired tumours and reference datasets (TCGA and CCLE). <sentence_start/>All plots were generated using ggplot2 (v3.3.5), with interactive features integrated using plotly (v4.9.3). <sentence_start/>The Clinical Module uses the swimplot package<citation rid="CR172" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.32614/CRAN.package.swimplot" count="1"><sup>172</sup></citation> to visualize patient treatment timelines and to track model treatment exposures. <sentence_start/>The application is deployed via Shiny Server, with all backend processing and analyses performed server-side. <sentence_start/>The source code for the app is available at GitHub ( ), and the hosted application can be accessed online ( ).
Ethics statement

All human tissue samples and associated clinical data used in this study were collected as part of the HCMI under protocols approved by the Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) of the respective Cancer Model Development Centres (CMDCs) and participating clinical sites. <sentence_start/>All procedures were conducted in accordance with relevant ethical guidelines and regulations. <sentence_start/>Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before sample collection, in accordance with HCMI programme requirements and institutional policies. <sentence_start/>Each participating centre fulfilled all regulatory requirements, including IRB-approved protocols, informed consent procedures and data-sharing agreements (Supplementary Note 2).
